Yaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ – ‘‘paccekā itthiyo āropetvā’’ti. Aparāpi soḷasasahassakhattiyanāṭakitthiyo rājānaṃ parivāresuṃ. Tāsaṃ pariyante khujjavāmanakakirātādayo. Tāsaṃ pariyante antepurapālakā vissāsikapurisā. Tesaṃ pariyante vicitravesavilāsino saṭṭhisahassamattā mahāmattā. Tesaṃ pariyante vividhālaṅkārapaṭimaṇḍitā nānappakāraāvudhahatthā vijjādharataruṇā viya navutisahassamattā raṭṭhiyaputtā. Tesaṃ pariyante satagghanikāni nivāsetvā pañcasatagghanikāni ekaṃsaṃ katvā sunhātā suvilittā kañcanamālādinānābharaṇasobhitā dasasahassamattā brāhmaṇā dakkhiṇahatthaṃ ussāpetvā jayasaddaṃ ghosantā gacchanti. Tesaṃ pariyante pañcaṅgikāni tūriyāni. Tesaṃ pariyante dhanupantiparikkhepo. Tassa pariyante hatthighaṭā. Hatthīnaṃ pariyante gīvāya gīvaṃ paharamānā assapanti. Assapariyante aññamaññaṃ saṅghaṭṭanarathā. Rathapariyante bāhāya bāhaṃ paharayamānā yodhā. Tesaṃ pariyante attano attano anurūpāya ābharaṇasampattiyā virocamānā aṭṭhārasa seniyo. Iti yathā pariyante ṭhatvā khitto saro rājānaṃ na pāpuṇāti, evaṃ jīvako komārabhacco rañño parisaṃ saṃvidahitvā attanā rañño avidūreneva gacchati – ‘‘sace koci upaddavo hoti, paṭhamatara rañño jīvitadānaṃ dassāmī’’ti. Ukkānaṃ pana ettakāni satāni vā sahassāni vāti paricchedo natthīti evarūpiṃ rājiddhiṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ – ‘‘mahaccarājānubhāvena yena jīvakassa komārabhaccassa ambavanaṃ, tena pāyāsī’’ti. Ahudeva bhayanti ettha cittutrāsabhayaṃ, ñāṇabhayaṃ, ārammaṇabhayaṃ, ottappabhayanti catubbidhaṃ bhayaṃ, tattha ‘‘jātiṃ paṭicca bhayaṃ bhayānaka’’ntiādinā nayena vuttaṃ cittutrāsabhayaṃ nāma. ‘‘Tepi tathāgatassa dhammadesanaṃ sutvā yebhuyyena bhayaṃ saṃvegaṃ santāsaṃ āpajjantī’’ti (saṃ. ni. 3.78) evamāgataṃ ñāṇabhayaṃ nāma. ‘‘Etaṃ nūna taṃ bhayabheravaṃ āgacchatī’’ti (ma. ni. 1.49) ettha vuttaṃ ārammaṇabhayaṃ nāma. Idaṃ ottappabhayaṃ nāma. Tesu idha cittutrāsabhayaṃ, ahu ahosīti attho. Chambhitattanti chambhitassa bhāvo. Sakalasarīracalananti attho. Lomahaṃsoti lomahaṃsanaṃ, uddhaṃ ṭhitalomatāti attho. So panāyaṃ lomahaṃso dhammassavanādīsu pītiuppattikāle pītiyāpi hoti . Bhīrukajātikānaṃ sampahārapisācādidassanesu bhayenāpi. Idha bhayalomahaṃsoti veditabbo. Kasmā panesa bhītoti? Andhakārenāti eke vadanti. Rājagahe kira dvattiṃsa mahādvārāni, catusaṭṭhi khuddakadvārāni. Jīvakassa ambavanaṃ pākārassa ca gijjhakūṭassa ca antarā hoti. So pācīnadvārena nikkhamitvā pabbatacchāyāya pāvisi, tattha pabbatakūṭena cando chādito, pabbatacchāyāya ca rukkhacchāyāya ca andhakāraṃ ahosīti, tampi akāraṇaṃ. Tadā hi ukkānaṃ satasahassānampi paricchedo natthi. Ayaṃ pana appasaddataṃ nissāya jīvake āsaṅkāya bhīto. Jīvako kirassa uparipāsādeyeva ārocesi – ‘‘mahārāja appasaddakāmo bhagavā, appasaddeneva upasaṅkamitabbo’’ti. Tasmā rājā tūriyasaddaṃ nivāresi. Tūriyāni kevalaṃ gahitamattāneva honti, vācampi uccaṃ anicchārayamānā accharāsaññāya gacchanti. Ambavanepi kassaci khipitasaddopi na suyyati. Rājāno ca nāma saddābhiratā honti. So taṃ appasaddataṃ nissāya ukkaṇṭhito jīvakepi āsaṅkaṃ uppādesi. ‘‘Ayaṃ jīvako mayhaṃ ambavane aḍḍhateḷasāni bhikkhusatānī’’ti āha. Ettha ca khipitasaddamattampi na suyyati, abhūtaṃ maññe, esa vañcetvā maṃ nagarato nīharitvā purato balakāyaṃ upaṭṭhapetvā maṃ gaṇhitvā attanā chattaṃ ussāpetukāmo. Ayañhi pañcannaṃ hatthīnaṃ balaṃ dhāreti. Mama ca avidūreneva gacchati, santike ca me āvudhahattho ekapurisopi natthi. Aho vata me anattho’’ti. Evaṃ bhāyitvā ca pana abhīto viya sandhāretumpi nāsakkhi. Attano bhītabhāvaṃ tassa āvi akāsi. Tena vuttaṃ. ‘‘Atha kho rājā…pe… na nigghoso’’ti. Tattha sammāti vayassābhilāpo esa, kacci maṃ vayassāti vuttaṃ hoti. Na palambhesīti yaṃ natthi taṃ atthīti vatvā kacci maṃ na vippalambhayasi. Nigghosoti kathāsallāpanigghoso. Mā bhāyi, mahārājāti jīvako – ‘‘ayaṃ rājā maṃ na jānāti ‘nāyaṃ paraṃ jīvitā voropetī’ti; sace kho pana naṃ na assāsessāmi, vinasseyyā’’ti cintayitvā daḷhaṃ katvā samassāsento ‘‘mā bhāyi mahārājā’’ti vatvā ‘‘na taṃ devā’’tiādimāha. Abhikkamāti abhimukho kama gaccha, pavisāti attho. Sakiṃ vutte pana daḷhaṃ na hotīti taramānova dvikkhattuṃ āha. Ete maṇḍalamāḷe dīpā jhāyantīti mahārāja, corabalaṃ nāma na dīpe jāletvā tiṭṭhati, ete ca maṇḍalamāḷe dīpā jalanti. Etāya dīpasaññāya yāhi mahārājāti vadati.
159.
Paccekā itthiyo means pāṭiyekkā itthiyo; it means that each elephant cow has one female.
Ukkāsu dhāriyamānāsu means daṇḍadīpikāsu dhāriyamānāsu (while torches are being carried means while torches on poles are being carried).
Mahacca rājānubhāvena means mahatā rājānubhāvena (with the great power of the king).
Mahaccātipi pāḷi, the meaning is mahati, this is a change of gender.
Rājānubhāvo is called rājiddhi (kingly power is called kingly success).
What is his rājiddhi? The glory of sovereignty over two great kingdoms of three hundred yojanas.
"On such and such a day, the king will approach the tathāgata," even if the preparations were not complete beforehand, at that very moment five hundred women, having taken the guise of men, with their veils removed, swords fastened to their shoulders, and holding jeweled staffs and tomaras, went out.
What was spoken with reference to that is: "Having made each woman mount."
Moreover, sixteen thousand dancing Kṣatriya women surrounded the king.
Around them were hunchbacks, dwarfs, Kirātas, and so on.
Around them were palace guards and trusted men.
Around them were sixty thousand great ministers, adorned with various costumes and finery.
Around them were ninety thousand royal sons, adorned with various ornaments and decorations, holding various kinds of weapons, like young vidyādharas.
Around them, having put on hundred-fold garments and having made five hundred-fold garments into a single shawl, well-bathed, well-anointed, adorned with various ornaments such as golden garlands, ten thousand brāhmaṇas, raising their right hands, went along shouting cries of victory.
Around them were five-piece orchestras.
Around them was a line of bows.
Around them were elephant troops.
Around the elephants, they snorted, striking neck against neck.
Around the horses were chariots colliding with each other.
Around the chariots were warriors striking arm against arm.
Around them were eighteen armies, shining with the wealth of ornaments corresponding to their own status.
Just as an arrow, shot having stood at the limit, does not reach the king, so Jīvaka Komārabhacca, having arranged the king's retinue, went along not far from the king himself, thinking: "If any danger arises, I will be the first to give the king the gift of life."
But there is no limit to the number of torches, whether hundreds or thousands, having referred to such kingly power, it was said: "With the great power of the king, by which he went to the mango grove of Jīvaka Komārabhacca, he was successful."
Here, "he was suddenly gripped by fear" refers to fear as mental anxiety, fear as knowledge, fear as a fearful object, and fear as moral dread, four kinds of fear. Among these, fear as mental anxiety is referred to in the passage: "In dependence on birth there arises fear, fright," etc.
“Those, having heard the Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dhamma, generally fall into fear, a sense of urgency, and terror” (Saṃ.
Ni.
3.
78) This is called knowledge of fear.
“Is this the fear and dread that is coming?” (Ma.
Ni.
1.
49) Here, what is spoken of is the fear of fearful objects.
This is called moral dread.
Among these, here fear as mental anxiety, happened, it means it happened.
Chambhitatta means the state of being startled.
Sakalasarīracalana means the movement of the whole body.
Lomahaṃso means lomahaṃsanaṃ, the hairs standing upwards, that is the meaning.
But that lomahaṃso also occurs through joy at the time of the arising of joy in hearing the Dharma and so on.
Also through fear in the visions of fearful kinds of ghosts and so on.
Here, it should be understood, signifies fear and bristling of the hair.

Why then is he afraid? Some say it is because of the darkness.

In Rājagaha, it is said, there are thirty-two great gates and sixty-four small gates.

Jīvaka’s Mango Grove is between the rampart and the Gijjhakūṭa (Vulture Peak).

He, having left by the eastern gate, entered into the shadow of the mountain. There, the moon was covered by the peak of the mountain, and because of the shadow of the mountain and the shadow of the trees, it was dark, but that too was without reason.

At that time, indeed, there was no limit even to hundreds of thousands of torches.

Because of the quietness, however, he was afraid, suspecting Jīvaka.

Jīvaka, it is said, had already announced to him in the upper terrace of the palace: “Great king, the Blessed One (bhagavā) is fond of quietness. He should be approached quietly.”

Therefore the king prohibited the sound of musical instruments (tūriyasaddaṃ).

The musical instruments (tūriyāni) were merely taken along. Also, they did not speak aloud, but went along giving signals with a snap of the fingers.

In the Mango Grove not even the sound of sneezing was heard.

And kings generally delight in sound.

Because of that quietness, he became uneasy, and he aroused suspicion even regarding Jīvaka.

“This Jīvaka told me there are twelve hundred and fifty monks (bhikkhus) in the Mango Grove,” he said.

And here not even the slightest sound of sneezing is heard. I think it is unreal. Wishing to deceive me, he has led me out of the city, set up an army in front, and intends to arrest me and raise his own umbrella, desiring kingship for himself.

For he has the strength of five elephants (hatthīnaṃ balaṃ dhāreti).

And he is going along not far from me, and there is not even a single armed man (āvudhahattho) near me.

“O, what harm has befallen me!”

Having become so much afraid, he could not conduct himself fearlessly.

He revealed his own fearfulness to him.

Therefore it has been said.

"Then the king…pe… no noise."

There, this is a friendly address, and it is as if it was said, "Are you well, friend?"

"You do not deceive," that is, saying that what is not, is, will you not deceive me?

"Noise" means the noise of friendly conversation (kathāsallāpanigghoso).

Jīvaka [said]: "Do not be afraid, great king (mahārāja)—this king does not know me; he does not know that I do not deprive another of life; but if I do not reassure him, he will perish," thinking thus, and making firm, reassuring him, and saying: "Do not be afraid, great king," he spoke beginning with "Not the gods..."

"Go forward" means go face to face, enter, is the meaning.

He says "Go forward" twice, hurrying along, because if he had said this once it would not be firm.

“These lamps are burning in the pavilion hall, great king (mahārāja). A group of thieves does not stay where lamps are burning. And these lamps are burning in the pavilion hall."

He says: "Go by this sign of the lamps, great king (mahārāja)."
160
160. Atha kho rājā māgadho ajātasattu vedehiputto yāvatikā nāgassa bhūmi nāgena gantvā, nāgā paccorohitvā, pattikova padikova (syā.) yena maṇḍalamāḷassa dvāraṃ tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā jīvakaṃ komārabhaccaṃ etadavoca – ‘‘kahaṃ pana, samma jīvaka, bhagavā’’ti? ‘‘Eso, mahārāja, bhagavā; eso, mahārāja, bhagavā majjhimaṃ thambhaṃ nissāya puratthābhimukho nisinno purakkhato bhikkhusaṅghassā’’ti.
Then, King Ajātaśatru, son of Vaidehī, having gone by elephant as far as the elephant's terrain (nāgassa bhūmi) extended, dismounted from the elephant (nāgā paccorohitvā), and approached on foot (pattikova padikova) the gate of the circular pavilion (maṇḍalamāḷassa dvāraṃ); having approached, he said to Jīvaka Komārabhacca, "Where, friend Jīvaka, is the Blessed One (bhagavā)?"
"Here, great king (mahārāja), is the Blessed One (bhagavā); here, great king, is the Blessed One (bhagavā), seated facing east, leaning against the central pillar (majjhimaṃ thambhaṃ nissāya), surrounded by the community of monks (bhikkhusaṅghassā)."
160.Nāgassa bhūmīti yattha sakkā hatthiṃ abhirūḷhena gantuṃ, ayaṃ nāgassa bhūmi nāma. Nāgā paccorohitvāti vihārassa bahidvārakoṭṭhake hatthito orohitvā. Bhūmiyaṃ patiṭṭhitasamakālameva pana bhagavato tejo rañño sarīraṃ phari. Athassa tāvadeva sakalasarīrato sedā mucciṃsu, sāṭakā pīḷetvā apanetabbā viya ahesuṃ. Attano aparādhaṃ saritvā mahābhayaṃ uppajji. So ujukaṃ bhagavato santikaṃ gantuṃ asakkonto jīvakaṃ hatthe gahetvā ārāmacārikaṃ caramāno viya ‘‘idaṃ te samma jīvaka suṭṭhu kāritaṃ idaṃ suṭṭhu kārita’’nti vihārassa vaṇṇaṃ bhaṇamāno anukkamena yena maṇḍalamāḷassa dvāraṃ tenupasaṅkami, sampattoti attho. Kahaṃ pana sammāti kasmā pucchīti. Eke tāva ‘‘ajānanto’’ti vadanti. Iminā kira daharakāle pitarā saddhiṃ āgamma bhagavā diṭṭhapubbo, pacchā pana pāpamittasaṃsaggena pitughātaṃ katvā abhimāre pesetvā dhanapālaṃ muñcāpetvā mahāparādho hutvā bhagavato sammukhībhāvaṃ na upagatapubboti asañjānanto pucchatīti. Taṃ akāraṇaṃ, bhagavā hi ākiṇṇavaralakkhaṇo anubyañjanapaṭimaṇḍito chabbaṇṇāhi rasmīhi sakalaṃ ārāmaṃ obhāsetvā tārāgaṇaparivuto viya puṇṇacando bhikkhugaṇaparivuto maṇḍalamāḷamajjhe nisinno, taṃ ko na jāneyya. Ayaṃ pana attano issariyalīlāya pucchati. Pakati hesā rājakulānaṃ, yaṃ jānantāpi ajānantā viya pucchanti. Jīvako pana taṃ sutvā – ‘ayaṃ rājā pathaviyaṃ ṭhatvā kuhiṃ pathavīti, nabhaṃ ulloketvā kuhiṃ candimasūriyāti, sinerumūle ṭhatvā kuhiṃ sinerūti vadamāno viya dasabalassa purato ṭhatvā kuhiṃ bhagavā’ti pucchati. ‘‘Handassa bhagavantaṃ dassessāmī’’ti cintetvā yena bhagavā tenañjaliṃ paṇāmetvā ‘‘eso mahārājā’’tiādimāha. Purakkhatoti parivāretvā nisinnassa purato nisinno.
160.
"Nāga’s ground" means a place where it is possible to go having mounted an elephant; this is called Nāga’s ground.
"Having dismounted from the nāga" means having dismounted from the elephant at the outer gatehouse of the monastery.
As soon as the king dismounted and set foot on the ground, the splendor of the Exalted One suffused his body.
Immediately, his entire body broke out into a sweat, and his clothes felt as though they should be removed, as if they were oppressing him.
Remembering his own crime, great fear arose in him.
He could not go directly to the Exalted One, but took Jīvaka by the hand and walked around as if touring the monastery grounds, saying: “You have built this well, Jīvaka, you have built this well.” Thus, praising the monastery, he gradually approached the door of the pavilion hall, meaning he arrived.
Why does he ask: “Where is the Exalted One?”
Some say: "Because he did not know."
They say that in his youth he had seen the Exalted One when he came along with his father; but afterwards, as a result of associating with evil friends, he killed his father, sent assassins, set the elephant Dhanapāla loose, and having thus become a great criminal, he did not meet the Exalted One face to face. Because of this, they say, he did not recognize him.
That is not the reason. For the Exalted One, sitting in the middle of the pavilion hall surrounded by the company of monks, appeared like the full moon surrounded by the host of stars. Marked with the most excellent bodily characteristics (ākiṇṇavaralakṣaṇo), adorned with the special features of physical beauty (anubyañjanapaṭimaṇḍito), he illuminated the entire monastery with his six-colored rays (chabbaṇṇāhi rasmīhi). Who would not have known him?
The king asks this as a mannerism of sovereignty.
For this is the nature of those of royal family; though knowing something, they ask as if they do not know.
But Jīvaka, having heard this question, thought to himself: “This king, standing on the earth, asks, ‘Where is the earth?’; or as if someone looking up at the sky were to ask, ‘Where are the sun and moon?’; or as if someone standing at the foot of Mount Meru were to ask, ‘Where is Meru?’; so, standing in front of the Ten-Powered One (dasabalassa), he asks, ‘Where is the Exalted One?’”
Thinking, "I will show him the Exalted One," making a reverential salutation (añjaliṃ paṇāmetvā) towards the Exalted One, he said: “That is the Exalted One, great king,” etc.
Purakkhato means one who is surrounded, sat in front of the one seated.
161
161. Atha kho rājā māgadho ajātasattu vedehiputto yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā ekamantaṃ aṭṭhāsi. Ekamantaṃ ṭhito kho rājā māgadho ajātasattu vedehiputto tuṇhībhūtaṃ tuṇhībhūtaṃ bhikkhusaṅghaṃ anuviloketvā rahadamiva vippasannaṃ udānaṃ udānesi – ‘‘iminā me upasamena udayabhaddo udāyibhaddo (sī. pī.) kumāro samannāgato hotu, yenetarahi upasamena bhikkhusaṅgho samannāgato’’ti. ‘‘Agamā kho tvaṃ, mahārāja, yathāpema’’nti. ‘‘Piyo me, bhante, udayabhaddo kumāro. Iminā me, bhante, upasamena udayabhaddo kumāro samannāgato hotu yenetarahi upasamena bhikkhusaṅgho samannāgato’’ti.
Then King Ajātaśatru, son of Videhi, of Magadha, approached the Blessed One; having approached, he stood to one side.

Standing to one side, King Ajātaśatru, son of Videhi, of Magadha, having surveyed the Saṅgha of monks in utter silence, as serene as a clear lake, exclaimed: "May Prince Udayabhadda be endowed with such tranquility as the Saṅgha of monks is endowed with now!"

"Do your thoughts, great king, follow the call of your affection?"

"Lord, Prince Udayabhadda is dear to me. May Prince Udayabhadda be endowed with such tranquility as the Saṅgha of monks is endowed with now!"
161.Yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkamīti yattha bhagavā tattha gato, bhagavato santikaṃ upagatoti attho. Ekamantaṃ aṭṭhāsīti bhagavantaṃ vā bhikkhusaṃghaṃ vā asaṅghaṭṭayamāno attano ṭhātuṃ anucchavike ekasmiṃ padese bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā ekova aṭṭhāsi. Tuṇhībhūtaṃ tuṇhībhūtanti yato yato anuviloketi, tato tato tuṇhībhūtamevāti attho. Tattha hi ekabhikkhussapi hatthakukkuccaṃ vā pādakukkuccaṃ vā khipitasaddo vā natthi, sabbālaṅkārapaṭimaṇḍitaṃ nāṭakaparivāraṃ bhagavato abhimukhe ṭhitaṃ rājānaṃ vā rājaparisaṃ vā ekabhikkhupi na olokesi. Sabbe bhagavantaṃyeva olokayamānā nisīdiṃsu. Rājā tesaṃ upasame pasīditvā vigatapaṅkatāya vippasannarahadamiva upasantindriyaṃ bhikkhusaṅghaṃ punappunaṃ anuviloketvā udānaṃ udānesi. Tattha imināti yena kāyikena ca vācasikena ca mānasikena ca sīlūpasamena bhikkhusaṅgho upasanto, iminā upasamenāti dīpeti. Tattha ‘‘aho vata me putto pabbajitvā ime bhikkhū viya upasanto bhaveyyā’’ti nayidaṃ sandhāya esa evamāha. Ayaṃ pana bhikkhusaṅghaṃ disvā pasanno puttaṃ anussari. Dullabhañhi laddhā acchariyaṃ vā disvā piyānaṃ ñātimittādīnaṃ anussaraṇaṃ nāma lokassa pakatiyeva. Iti bhikkhusaṅghaṃ disvā puttaṃ anussaramāno esa evamāha. Api ca putte āsaṅkāya tassa upasamaṃ icchamāno pesa evamāha. Evaṃ kirassa ahosi, putto me pucchissati – ‘‘mayhaṃ pitā daharo. Ayyako me kuhi’’nti. So ‘‘pitarā te ghātito’’ti sutvā ‘‘ahampi pitaraṃ ghātetvā rajjaṃ kāressāmī’’ti maññissati. Iti putte āsaṅkāya tassa upasamaṃ icchamāno pesa evamāha. Kiñcāpi hi esa evamāha. Atha kho naṃ putto ghātessatiyeva. Tasmiñhi vaṃse pituvadho pañcaparivaṭṭe gato. Ajātasattu bimbisāraṃ ghātesi, udayo ajātasattuṃ . Tassa putto mahāmuṇḍiko nāma udayaṃ. Tassa putto anuruddho nāma mahāmuṇḍikaṃ. Tassa putto nāgadāso nāma anuruddhaṃ. Nāgadāsaṃ pana – ‘‘vaṃsacchedakarājāno ime, kiṃ imehī’’ti raṭṭhavāsino kupitā ghātesuṃ. Agamā kho tvanti kasmā evamāha? Bhagavā kira rañño vacībhede akateyeva cintesi – ‘‘ayaṃ rājā āgantvā tuṇhī niravo ṭhito, kiṃ nu kho cintesī’’ti. Athassa cittaṃ ñatvā – ‘‘ayaṃ mayā saddhiṃ sallapituṃ asakkonto bhikkhusaṅghaṃ anuviloketvā puttaṃ anussari, na kho panāyaṃ mayi anālapante kiñci kathetuṃ sakkhissati, karomi tena saddhiṃ kathāsallāpa’’nti. Tasmā rañño vacanānantaraṃ ‘‘agamā kho tvaṃ, mahārāja, yathāpema’’nti āha. Tassattho – mahārāja, yathā nāma unname vuṭṭhaṃ udakaṃ yena ninnaṃ tena gacchati, evameva tvaṃ bhikkhusaṅghaṃ anuviloketvā yena pemaṃ tena gatoti. Atha rañño etadahosi – ‘‘aho acchariyā buddhaguṇā, mayā sadiso bhagavato aparādhakārako nāma natthi, mayā hissa aggupaṭṭhāko ghātito, devadattassa ca kathaṃ gahetvā abhimārā pesitā, nāḷāgiri mutto, maṃ nissāya devadattena silā paviddhā, evaṃ mahāparādhaṃ nāma maṃ ālapato dasabalassa mukhaṃ nappahoti; aho bhagavā pañcahākārehi tādilakkhaṇe suppatiṭṭhito. Evarūpaṃ nāma satthāraṃ pahāya bahiddhā na pariyesissāmā’’ti so somanassajāto bhagavantaṃ ālapanto ‘‘piyo me, bhante’’tiādimāha.
161.
Because he approached the Blessed One means: where the Blessed One was, there he went; the meaning is that he went into the presence of the Blessed One.

Standing to one side means that, without obstructing the Blessed One or the monastic community, he stood in a suitable place, respectfully saluted the Blessed One, and stood alone.

"Being silent" means that wherever he looked around, he was simply silent, this is the meaning.

There, not even one bhikkhu played with his hands (hatthakukkuccaṃ) or feet (pādakukkuccaṃ) or made a cracking sound. Not even one bhikkhu looked at the king or his assembly standing in front of the Blessed One, or at the retinue of nautch-girls adorned with all their ornaments (sabbālaṅkāra-paṭimaṇḍitaṃ nāṭaka-parivāraṃ).

All sat there, looking only at the Exalted One ( bhagavantaṃ).

The king, gaining confidence in such peace, again and again surveyed the company of bhikkhus sitting there with calm faculties, like a clear lake free from mud, and then uttered his joyful exclamation ( udānaṃ udānesi):

There, "by this" means that the monastic community is peaceful through bodily, verbal, mental, and ethical peace; "by this peace" is what is indicated.

There, he did not say this intending: “O, may my son go forth and become peaceful like these bhikkhus!”

Rather, having gained confidence seeing the company of bhikkhus, he remembered his son.

For that is the nature of people in the world: when they have gained something rare or seen something wonderful, they remember their dear relatives and friends (ñātimittādīnaṃ).

Thus, having gained confidence seeing the monastic community, he remembered his son, and spoke thus.

Moreover, he said this because he was apprehensive about his son and desired peace for him.

For he thought: “My son will ask: ‘My father is young.

Where is my grandfather?’"

Hearing ‘Your father killed him’, he might think: ‘Then I shall kill my father and rule the kingdom!’

Thus, apprehensive about his son, he spoke thus desiring this peace for him.

Yet though he said this,

his son eventually killed him.

In that dynasty parricide took place in five generations.

Ajātaśatru killed Bimbisāra; Udaya killed Ajātaśatru;

Udayi was killed by his own son, Mahāmuṇḍika;

Mahāmuṇḍika was killed by his son Anuruddha;

and Anuruddha was killed by his son Nāgadāsa.

But the citizens became angry and thinking, “These kings destroy their own lineage; what do we need them for?” they killed Nāgadāsa.

Why did he speak thus, “You have come well”? It is said that before the king uttered his exclamation, the Exalted One had thought: “The king, having come, stands here silent and speechless. What is he thinking?”

Having read his mind, he reflected: “Being unable to converse with me, he surveys the monastic community and remembers his son. Since he will be unable to say anything if I do not speak to him first, I will start a conversation with him.”

Therefore, immediately after the king uttered his joyful exclamation, the Exalted One spoke the above words.

This is the meaning: “Great king, as rain water, falling upon the highlands, flows down to the plain, so as you survey the company of bhikkhus, your affection goes towards your son.”

Thereupon the king thought: “O, how wonderful are the virtues of the Buddha! There is no one who has committed such crimes towards the Exalted One as I have. I killed his chief supporter; I accepted the request of Devadatta and sent assassins to kill him; I released the elephant Nālāgiri against him; with my support Devadatta hurled a stone at him. The Buddha should not even open his mouth towards such a criminal as myself, yet he freely addresses me. O, the Exalted One is well-established in the five aspects of suchness (pañcahākārehi tādilakkhaṇe suppatiṭṭhito).

I should not abandon such a teacher and search for a teacher elsewhere.” Filled with joy (somanassajāto), addressing the Exalted One (bhagavantaṃ ālapanto), he said: “Venerable sir (bhante), I love my son,” etc.
162
162. Atha kho rājā māgadho ajātasattu vedehiputto bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā, bhikkhusaṅghassa añjaliṃ paṇāmetvā , ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Ekamantaṃ nisinno kho rājā māgadho ajātasattu vedehiputto bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – ‘‘puccheyyāmahaṃ, bhante, bhagavantaṃ kiñcideva desaṃ kiñcideva desaṃ lesamattaṃ (syā. kaṃ. ka.); sace me bhagavā okāsaṃ karoti pañhassa veyyākaraṇāyā’’ti. ‘‘Puccha, mahārāja, yadākaṅkhasī’’ti.
162. Then King Ajātaśatru, son of Videhi, having respectfully saluted the Blessed One and saluted the Order of Monks with joined hands, sat down to one side.

Having sat down to one side, King Ajātaśatru, son of Videhi, said this to the Blessed One: "Venerable sir, I would like to ask the Blessed One about a certain point, a trifling matter; if the Blessed One would grant me the opportunity to explain my question."

"Ask, great king, whatever you wish."
162.Bhikkhusaṅghassaañjaliṃ paṇāmetvāti evaṃ kirassa ahosi bhagavantaṃ vanditvā itocito ca gantvā bhikkhusaṅghaṃ vandantena ca bhagavā piṭṭhito kātabbo hoti, garukāropi cesa na hoti. Rājānaṃ vanditvā uparājānaṃ vandantenapi hi rañño agāravo kato hoti. Tasmā bhagavantaṃ vanditvā ṭhitaṭṭhāneyeva bhikkhusaṅghassa añjaliṃ paṇāmetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Kañcideva desanti kañci okāsaṃ. Athassa bhagavā pañhapucchane ussāhaṃ janento āha – ‘‘puccha, mahārāja, yadākaṅkhasī’’ti. Tassattho – ‘‘puccha yadi ākaṅkhasi, na me pañhavissajjane bhāro atthi’’. Atha vā ‘‘puccha, yaṃ ākaṅkhasi, sabbaṃ te vissajjessāmī’’ti sabbaññupavāraṇaṃ pavāresi, asādhāraṇaṃ paccekabuddhaaggasāvakamahāsāvakehi. Te hi yadākaṅkhasīti na vadanti, sutvā vedissāmāti vadanti. Buddhā pana – ‘‘puccha, āvuso, yadākaṅkhasī’’ti (saṃ. ni. 1.237), vā ‘‘puccha, mahārāja, yadākaṅkhasī’’ti vā, Tena hi tvaṃ, bhikkhu, sake āsane nisīditvā puccha, yadākaṅkhasīti vā, Tesaṃ tesaṃ yakkhanarindadevasamaṇabrāhmaṇaparibbājakānaṃ sabbaññupavāraṇaṃ pavārenti. Anacchariyañcetaṃ, yaṃ bhagavā buddhabhūmiṃ patvā etaṃ pavāraṇaṃ pavāreyya. Yo bodhisattabhūmiyaṃ padesañāṇe ṭhito – Evaṃ sakkādīnaṃ atthāya isīhi yācito – Evaṃ sarabhaṅgakāle. Sambhavajātake ca sakalajambudīpaṃ tikkhattuṃ vicaritvā pañhānaṃ antakaraṃ adisvā suciratena brāhmaṇena, pañhaṃ puṭṭhuṃ okāse kārite jātiyā sattavassiko rathikāya paṃsuṃ kīḷanto pallaṅkamābhujitvā antaravīthiyaṃ nisinnova –
162. "Having bowed to the Order of Monks": Thus, it occurred to him, "Having bowed to the Blessed One, and then having gone here and there, if one bows to the Order of Monks, the Blessed One would be behind [them], and this would not be showing due respect."

Having bowed to the king, even when bowing to the sub-king, disrespect has been shown to the king.

Therefore, having bowed to the Blessed One, and remaining in the same place, having bowed to the Order of Monks, he sat down to one side.

They teach some teaching, some opportunity.

Then, the Blessed One, generating enthusiasm for asking a question, said to him: "Ask, great king, whatever you wish (yadākaṅkhasī)."

Its meaning is: "Ask if you wish (ākāṅkhasi); there is no burden to me in answering questions."

Or, "Ask, whatever you wish (yaṃ ākaṅkhasi), I will answer everything (sabbaṃ te vissajjessāmī)," thus, the Blessed One extended the invitation of the all-knowing (sabbaññupavāraṇaṃ), uncommon to individual Buddhas, chief disciples and great disciples.

For they do not say, "Ask whatever you wish (yadākaṅkhasīti)," but they say, "Having heard, we will try to answer."

But Buddhas say: "Ask, friend (āvuso), whatever you wish (yadākaṅkhasī)" (Saṃ. Ni. 1.237), or "Ask, great king, whatever you wish (yadākaṅkhasī)" or, "Therefore, you, bhikkhu, having sat down on your own seat, ask, whatever you wish (yadākaṅkhasī)," they extend the invitation of the all-knowing (sabbaññupavāraṇaṃ) to those yakṣas, kings of men, gods, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and wanderers (parivrājakas).

It is not wonderful that the Blessed One, having attained the Buddha-ground (buddhabhūmiṃ), would extend this invitation (pavāraṇaṃ).

He who is situated in the knowledge of a region (padesañāṇe) on the Bodhisattva-ground (bodhisattabhūmiyaṃ) - thus, requested by seers (ṛṣis) for the benefit of Śakra and others - thus, at the time of Sarabhaṅga.

And in the Sambhava Jātaka, having travelled three times through the whole Jambudvīpa, not seeing an end to the questions, after a long time, by a brāhmaṇa, having caused an opportunity for asking a question, a seven-year-old by birth, while playing with dust on the road, folding his legs, was seated in the middle of the street -
163
163. ‘‘Yathā nu kho imāni, bhante, puthusippāyatanāni, seyyathidaṃ – hatthārohā assārohā rathikā dhanuggahā celakā calakā piṇḍadāyakā uggā rājaputtā pakkhandino mahānāgā sūrā cammayodhino dāsikaputtā āḷārikā kappakā nhāpakā nahāpikā (sī.), nhāpikā (syā.) sūdā mālākārā rajakā pesakārā naḷakārā kumbhakārā gaṇakā muddikā, yāni vā panaññānipi evaṃgatāni puthusippāyatanāni, te diṭṭheva dhamme sandiṭṭhikaṃ sippaphalaṃ upajīvanti; te tena attānaṃ sukhenti pīṇenti pīnenti (katthaci), mātāpitaro sukhenti pīṇenti, puttadāraṃ sukhenti pīṇenti, mittāmacce sukhenti pīṇenti, samaṇabrāhmaṇesu samaṇesu brāhmaṇesu (ka.) uddhaggikaṃ dakkhiṇaṃ patiṭṭhapenti sovaggikaṃ sukhavipākaṃ saggasaṃvattanikaṃ. Sakkā nu kho, bhante, evameva diṭṭheva dhamme sandiṭṭhikaṃ sāmaññaphalaṃ paññapetu’’nti?
“Venerable sir, just as there are these various diverse crafts, such as elephant trainers (hatthārohā), horse trainers (assārohā), charioteers (rathikā), archers (dhanuggahā), standard bearers (celakā), camp marshals (calakā), army caterers (piṇḍadāyakā), champions and senior officers (uggā rājaputtā), front-line soldiers (pakkhandino mahānāgā), heroes (sūrā), cuirassiers (cammayodhino), slaves’ sons (dāsikaputtā), confectioners (āḷārikā), barbers (kappakā), bath attendants (nhāpakā), cooks (sūdā), garland-makers (mālākārā), laundrymen (rajakā), weavers (pesakārā), basket-makers (naḷakārā), potters (kumbhakārā), calculators (gaṇakā) and accountants (muddikā)—and whatever other skills there are of a similar nature: they enjoy here and now the visible fruits of their skills (sandiṭṭhikaṃ sippaphalaṃ); they delight and gratify themselves thereby, they delight and gratify their mothers and fathers, they delight and gratify their children and spouses, they delight and gratify their friends and colleagues, they establish an uplifting donation among ascetics and Brahmins, conducive to heaven, resulting in happiness, and leading to heaven. Is it possible, venerable sir, to point out any fruit of the ascetic life (sāmaññaphalaṃ) that is similarly visible here and now (sandiṭṭhikaṃ)?”
163. Evaṃ bhagavatā sabbaññupavāraṇāya pavāritāya attamano rājā pañhaṃ pucchanto – ‘‘yathā nu kho imāni, bhante’’tiādimāha. Tattha sippameva sippāyatanaṃ. Puthusippāyatanānīti bahūni sippāni. Seyyathidanti katame pana te. Hatthārohātiādīhi ye taṃ taṃ sippaṃ nissāya jīvanti, te dasseti. Ayañhi assādhippāyo – ‘‘yathā imesaṃ sippūpajīvīnaṃ taṃ taṃ sippaṃ nissāya sandiṭṭhikaṃ sippaphalaṃ paññāyati. Sakkā nu kho evaṃ sandiṭṭhikaṃ sāmaññaphalaṃ paññāpetu’’nti. Tasmā sippāyatanāni āharitvā sippūpajīvino dasseti. Tattha hatthārohāti sabbepi hatthācariyahatthivejjahatthimeṇḍādayo dasseti. Assārohāti sabbepi assācariyaassavejjaassameṇḍādayo. Rathikāti sabbepi rathācariyarathayodharatharakkhādayo. Dhanuggahāti dhanuācariyā issāsā. Celakāti ye yuddhe jayadhajaṃ gahetvā purato gacchanti. Calakāti idha rañño ṭhānaṃ hotu, idha asukamahāmattassāti evaṃ senābyūhakārakā. Piṇḍadāyakāti sāhasikamahāyodhā. Te kira parasenaṃ pavisitvā parasīsaṃ piṇḍamiva chetvā chetvā dayanti, uppatitvā uppatitvā niggacchantīti attho. Ye vā saṅgāmamajjhe yodhānaṃ bhattapātiṃ gahetvā parivisanti, tesampetaṃ nāmaṃ. Uggārājaputtāti uggatuggatā saṅgāmāvacarā rājaputtā. Pakkhandinoti ye ‘‘kassa sīsaṃ vā āvudhaṃ vā āharāmā’’ti ‘‘vatvā asukassā’’ti vuttā saṅgāmaṃ pakkhanditvā tadeva āharanti, ime pakkhandantīti pakkhandino. Mahānāgāti mahānāgā viya mahānāgā, hatthiādīsupi abhimukhaṃ āgacchantesu anivattitayodhānametaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Sūrāti ekantasūrā, ye sajālikāpi sacammikāpi samuddaṃ tarituṃ sakkonti. Cammayodhinoti ye cammakañcukaṃ vā pavisitvā saraparittāṇacammaṃ vā gahetvā yujjhanti. Dāsikaputtāti balavasinehā gharadāsayodhā. Āḷārikāti pūvikā. Kappakāti nhāpikā. Nhāpakāti ye nhāpenti. Sūdāti bhattakārakā. Mālākārādayo pākaṭāyeva. Gaṇakāti acchiddakapāṭhakā. Muddikāti hatthamuddāya gaṇanaṃ nissāya jīvino. Yāni vā panaññānipīti ayakāradantakāracittakārādīni. Evaṃgatānīti evaṃ pavattāni. Te diṭṭheva dhammeti te hatthārohādayo tāni puthusippāyatanāni dassetvā rājakulato mahāsampattiṃ labhamānā sandiṭṭhikameva sippaphalaṃ upajīvanti. Sukhentīti sukhitaṃ karonti. Pīṇentīti pīṇitaṃ thāmabalūpetaṃ karonti. Uddhaggikādīsu upari phalanibbattanato uddhaṃ aggamassā atthīti uddhaggikā. Saggaṃ arahatīti sovaggikā. Sukho vipāko assāti sukhavipākā. Suṭṭhu agge rūpasaddagandharasaphoṭṭhabbaāyuvaṇṇasukhayasaādhipateyyasaṅkhāte dasa dhamme saṃvatteti nibbattetīti saggasaṃvattanikā. Taṃ evarūpaṃ dakkhiṇaṃ dānaṃ patiṭṭhapentīti attho. Sāmaññaphalanti ettha paramatthato maggo sāmaññaṃ. Ariyaphalaṃ sāmaññaphalaṃ. Yathāha – ‘‘katamañca, bhikkhave, sāmaññaṃ? Ayameva ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo. Seyyathidaṃ, sammādiṭṭhi…pe… sammāsamādhi. Idaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, sāmaññaṃ. Katamāni ca, bhikkhave, sāmaññaphalāni? Sotāpattiphalaṃ…pe… arahattaphala’’nti (saṃ. ni. 5.35). Taṃ esa rājā na jānāti. Upari āgataṃ pana dāsakassakopamaṃ sandhāya pucchati. Atha bhagavā pañhaṃ avissajjetvāva cintesi – ‘‘ime bahū aññatitthiyasāvakā rājāmaccā idhāgatā, te kaṇhapakkhañca sukkapakkhañca dīpetvā kathīyamāne amhākaṃ rājā mahantena ussāhena idhāgato, tassāgatakālato paṭṭhāya samaṇo gotamo samaṇakolāhalaṃ samaṇabhaṇḍanameva kathetīti ujjhāyissanti, na sakkaccaṃ dhammaṃ sossanti, raññā pana kathīyamāne ujjhāyituṃ na sakkhissanti, rājānameva anuvattissanti. Issarānuvattako hi loko. ‘Handāhaṃ raññova bhāraṃ karomī’ti rañño bhāraṃ karonto ‘‘abhijānāsi no tva’’ntiādimāha.
163. Thus, when the Exalted One had invited him to ask with the invitation of an Omniscient One, the elated king asked his question, beginning with, "Just as these, venerable sir..."
There, skill itself is a place of skill (śilpāyatana).
"Various places of skill" means many skills.
"Namely this" means which ones are they?
He indicates those who live by relying on that particular skill, beginning with elephant trainers (hatthāroha).
For this is his intention: "Just as a visible fruit of skill is discerned for those who live by these skills by relying on that particular skill."
"Is it possible to point out any visible fruit of recluseship (sāmaññaphala) in this way?"
Therefore, having brought forward the places of skill, he indicates those who live by those skills.
There, hatthāroha means he indicates all of the elephant trainers, elephant doctors, and elephant tamers, and so forth.
Assāroha means all of the horse trainers, horse doctors, and horse tamers, and so forth.
Rathika means all of the chariot trainers, chariot warriors, and chariot protectors, and so forth.
Dhanuggaha means bow masters and archers (iṣvāsa).
Celaka means those who go in front, taking the victory banner in battle.
Calaka means those who arrange the battle array, [saying,] "Let there be a place for the king here; let there be [a place] for such-and-such a great minister here."
Piṇḍadāyaka means courageous great warriors.
It means that they enter the enemy's army and strike down the enemy's leaders, cutting them down as if [they were] morsels, leaping up and leaping up, and going out.
Or, those who, in the midst of battle, take a food bowl and serve the warriors—this is their name.
Uggārājaputta means the princes who are fierce and have access to battles.
Pakkhandino means those who, having said, "Let us bring the head or weapon of whomever," and having been told, "of so-and-so," leap into battle and bring just that, these are called pakkhandino because they leap.
Mahānāga means great warriors, like great elephants; this is a designation for warriors who do not turn back when facing elephants and so forth as they approach.
Sūra means those who are completely brave, who are able to cross the ocean even with nets and hides.
Cammayodhino means those who enter a leather coat of mail or fight taking a shield of hide that protects from arrows.
Dāsikaputta means household slave warriors who are strong and affectionate.
Āḷārika means cooks.
Kappaka means barbers (nhāpika).
Nhāpaka means those who shave (nhāpenti).
Sūda means makers of food (bhattakāraka).
Garland makers (mālākāra) and so forth are well-known.
Gaṇaka means uninterrupted reciters.
Muddika means those who live by relying on calculation with hand seals.
Or, whatever other [skills there may be], such as ironworkers, ivory workers, and painters (cittakāra), and so forth.
"Being thus gone" means being thus proceeded.
They, in the very visible dharma, those elephant trainers and so forth, having shown those various places of skill, and obtaining great wealth from the royal family, live by just the visible fruit of skill.
"They gladden" means they make [others] happy.
"They strengthen" means they make [others] strong and endowed with power and strength.
Among uddhaggika and so forth, because the top of it has fruit produced above, [and] the top of it exists, it is called uddhaggika.
Because it is worthy of heaven (svarga), it is called sovaggika.
Because its result (vipāka) is pleasant, it is called sukhavipāka.
Because it well converts and produces the ten dharmas that are called form (rūpa), sound (śabda), smell (gandha), taste (rasa), touch (spoṭṭhabba), life (āyu), color (varṇa), happiness (sukha), fame (yaśas), and sovereignty (ādhipateyya) at the top, it is called svargasaṃvartanika.
That is, they establish such a দক্ষিণা dakkhiṇā offering or gift; this is the meaning.

“Sāmaññaphala”—here, in the ultimate sense, magga (the path) is sāmañña (recluseship).

Ariyaphalaṃ sāmaññaphalaṃ: and the noble fruit is the fruit of recluseship.

As he said: “What, monks, is sāmañña (recluseship)? It is just this noble eightfold path (ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo), that is, right view (sammā-diṭṭhi)…pe… right concentration (sammā-samādhi).

This, monks, is called sāmañña (recluseship).

What, monks, are the fruits of recluseship (sāmaññaphalāni)? The fruit of stream-entry (sotāpattiphalaṃ)…pe… the fruit of arahat (arahattaphala)…” (Saṃ.
Ni.
5.
35).

The king does not know that.

He asks, referring to the simile of the servant and the farmer who came above.

Then, the Blessed One, without answering the question, thought: "These many disciples of other sects, royal ministers, have come here. If, while they are speaking, I were to explain the dark side (kaṇhapakkha) and the bright side (sukkapakkha), they would complain, 'Our king has come here with great enthusiasm, but from the time he arrived, the ascetic Gotama only speaks of the quarrels and disputes of ascetics.' They will not listen respectfully to the Dharma, but if it is spoken by the king, they will not be able to complain and will follow the king.

For in the world (loko), people follow those in power (issara).

'So, let me give the burden to the king,' thinking thus, while giving the burden to the king, he said, "Do you remember, great king, ever asking other recluses and brahmins this question?" etc.
164
164. ‘‘Abhijānāsi no tvaṃ, mahārāja, imaṃ pañhaṃ aññe samaṇabrāhmaṇe pucchitā’’ti ? ‘‘Abhijānāmahaṃ, bhante, imaṃ pañhaṃ aññe samaṇabrāhmaṇe pucchitā’’ti. ‘‘Yathā kathaṃ pana te, mahārāja, byākariṃsu, sace te agaru bhāsassū’’ti. ‘‘Na kho me, bhante, garu, yatthassa bhagavā nisinno, bhagavantarūpo vā’’ti cāti (sī. ka.). ‘‘Tena hi, mahārāja, bhāsassū’’ti.
164.
“Do you remember, great king, ever asking other śramaṇa mendicants and brāhmaṇa priests this question?” “Yes, venerable sir, I remember asking other śramaṇa mendicants and brāhmaṇa priests this question.”
“If it isn’t troublesome for you, great king, please tell us how they answered.”
“It is not troublesome for me, venerable sir, when the Exalted One (bhagavā) or anyone like him is present.”
ka.
"Well then, great king, tell me."
164. Tattha abhijānāsi no tvanti abhijānāsi nu tvaṃ. Ayañca no-saddo parato pucchitāti padena yojetabbo. Idañhi vuttaṃ hoti – ‘‘mahārāja, tvaṃ imaṃ pañhaṃ aññe samaṇabrāhmaṇe pucchitā nu, abhijānāsi ca naṃ puṭṭhabhāvaṃ, na te sammuṭṭha’’nti. Sace te agarūti sace tuyhaṃ yathā te byākariṃsu, tathā idha bhāsituṃ bhāriyaṃ na hoti, yadi na koci aphāsukabhāvo atthi, bhāsassūti attho. Na kho me bhanteti kiṃ sandhāyāha? Paṇḍitapatirūpakānañhi santike kathetuṃ dukkhaṃ hoti, te pade pade akkhare akkhare dosameva vadanti. Ekantapaṇḍitā pana kathaṃ sutvā sukathitaṃ pasaṃsanti, dukkathitesu pāḷipadaatthabyañjanesu yaṃ yaṃ virujjhati, taṃ taṃ ujukaṃ katvā denti. Bhagavatā ca sadiso ekantapaṇḍito nāma natthi. Tenāha – ‘‘na kho me, bhante, garu; yatthassa bhagavā nisinno bhagavantarūpo vā’’ti.
164.
There, do you recognize or not? Do you recognize, indeed?
And this particle "no" should be connected with the word "questioned" later on.
For it was said: "Great king, did you ask other śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas this question? And do you recognize the state of being questioned? You are not confused."
If it is not troublesome for you—if as they explained to you, so to speak here is not burdensome—if there is no discomfort, the meaning is, speak!
Why did he say, "It is not troublesome for me, venerable sir?" For it is difficult to speak in the presence of those who merely resemble wise men, for they only find fault in every word and every syllable.
But how do the truly wise men, having heard, praise what is well-spoken? And when something contradicts the meaning and phrasing of the Pāli texts in what is wrongly spoken, they correct it and give it straightforwardly.
And there is no truly wise man equal to the Blessed One (Bhagavat).
Therefore he said, "It is not troublesome for me, venerable sir, where the Exalted One (bhagavā), or one resembling the Exalted One, is seated."
165
165. ‘‘Ekamidāhaṃ, bhante, samayaṃ yena pūraṇo kassapo tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā pūraṇena kassapena saddhiṃ sammodiṃ. Sammodanīyaṃ kathaṃ sāraṇīyaṃ vītisāretvā ekamantaṃ nisīdiṃ. Ekamantaṃ nisinno kho ahaṃ, bhante, pūraṇaṃ kassapaṃ etadavocaṃ – ‘yathā nu kho imāni, bho kassapa, puthusippāyatanāni, seyyathidaṃ – hatthārohā assārohā rathikā dhanuggahā celakā calakā piṇḍadāyakā uggā rājaputtā pakkhandino mahānāgā sūrā cammayodhino dāsikaputtā āḷārikā kappakā nhāpakā sūdā mālākārā rajakā pesakārā naḷakārā kumbhakārā gaṇakā muddikā, yāni vā panaññānipi evaṃgatāni puthusippāyatanāni- te diṭṭheva dhamme sandiṭṭhikaṃ sippaphalaṃ upajīvanti; te tena attānaṃ sukhenti pīṇenti, mātāpitaro sukhenti pīṇenti, puttadāraṃ sukhenti pīṇenti, mittāmacce sukhenti pīṇenti, samaṇabrāhmaṇesu uddhaggikaṃ dakkhiṇaṃ patiṭṭhapenti sovaggikaṃ sukhavipākaṃ saggasaṃvattanikaṃ. Sakkā nu kho, bho kassapa, evameva diṭṭheva dhamme sandiṭṭhikaṃ sāmaññaphalaṃ paññapetu’nti?
“Once, venerable sir, I approached Pūraṇa Kassapa; having approached him, I exchanged greetings with Pūraṇa Kassapa. After exchanging courteous greetings and amiable talk, I sat down to one side.

Having sat down to one side, venerable sir, I said this to Pūraṇa Kassapa: ‘Just as there are these various crafts, good Kassapa, such as elephant trainers (hatthārohā), horse trainers (assārohā), charioteers (rathikā), archers (dhanuggahā), standard bearers (celakā), camp marshals (calakā), army caterers (piṇḍadāyakā), champions and senior officers (uggā rājaputtā), scouts (pakkhandino), heroes (mahānāgā), brave fighters (sūrā), cuirassiers (cammayodhino), slaves’ sons (dāsikaputtā), cooks (āḷārikā), barbers (kappakā), bathmen (nhāpakā), bakers (sūdā), garland-makers (mālākārā), bleachers (rajakā), weavers (pesakārā), basket-makers (naḷakārā), potters (kumbhakārā), calculators (gaṇakā) and accountants (muddikā) — and whatever other skills there are: they enjoy here and now the visible fruits of their skills (diṭṭheva dhamme sandiṭṭhikaṃ sippaphalaṃ upajīvanti); by these means they gladden and gratify themselves, gladden and gratify their mothers and fathers, gladden and gratify their children and wives, gladden and gratify their friends and associates, and they establish an uplifting offering for ascetics and Brahmins, conducive to heavenly results of happiness, and leading to heaven.

Is it possible, good Kassapa, to point out any fruit of recluseship (sāmaññaphalaṃ) visible here and now (diṭṭheva dhamme sandiṭṭhikaṃ) in just the same way?"
165.Ekamidāhanti ekaṃ idha ahaṃ. Sammodanīyaṃ kathaṃ sāraṇīyaṃ vītisāretvāti sammodajanakaṃ saritabbayuttakaṃ kathaṃ pariyosāpetvā.
165.
"One" means, "I strike one here."
How, after completely concluding what is agreeable, what should be made to run, what should be removed, what generates joy, and what is connected to what should flow?
166
166. ‘‘Evaṃ vutte, bhante, pūraṇo kassapo maṃ etadavoca – ‘karoto kho, mahārāja, kārayato, chindato chedāpayato, pacato pācāpayato socayato, socāpayato, kilamato kilamāpayato, phandato phandāpayato, pāṇamatipātāpayato, adinnaṃ ādiyato, sandhiṃ chindato, nillopaṃ harato, ekāgārikaṃ karoto, paripanthe tiṭṭhato, paradāraṃ gacchato, musā bhaṇato, karoto na karīyati pāpaṃ. Khurapariyantena cepi cakkena yo imissā pathaviyā pāṇe ekaṃ maṃsakhalaṃ ekaṃ maṃsapuñjaṃ kareyya, natthi tatonidānaṃ pāpaṃ, natthi pāpassa āgamo. Dakkhiṇaṃ cepi gaṅgāya tīraṃ gaccheyya hananto ghātento chindanto chedāpento pacanto pācāpento, natthi tatonidānaṃ pāpaṃ, natthi pāpassa āgamo. Uttarañcepi gaṅgāya tīraṃ gaccheyya dadanto dāpento yajanto yajāpento, natthi tatonidānaṃ puññaṃ, natthi puññassa āgamo. Dānena damena saṃyamena saccavajjena natthi puññaṃ, natthi puññassa āgamo’ti. Itthaṃ kho me, bhante, pūraṇo kassapo sandiṭṭhikaṃ sāmaññaphalaṃ puṭṭho samāno akiriyaṃ byākāsi. ‘‘Seyyathāpi, bhante, ambaṃ vā puṭṭho labujaṃ byākareyya , labujaṃ vā puṭṭho ambaṃ byākareyya; evameva kho me, bhante, pūraṇo kassapo sandiṭṭhikaṃ sāmaññaphalaṃ puṭṭho samāno akiriyaṃ byākāsi. Tassa mayhaṃ, bhante, etadahosi – ‘kathañhi nāma mādiso samaṇaṃ vā brāhmaṇaṃ vā vijite vasantaṃ apasādetabbaṃ maññeyyā’ti. So kho ahaṃ, bhante, pūraṇassa kassapassa bhāsitaṃ neva abhinandiṃ nappaṭikkosiṃ. Anabhinanditvā appaṭikositvā anattamano, anattamanavācaṃ anicchāretvā, tameva vācaṃ anuggaṇhanto anikkujjanto anikkujjento (syā. kaṃ. ka.) uṭṭhāyāsanā pakkamiṃ pakkāmiṃ (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.).
166.

When this was said, venerable sir, Pūraṇa Kassapa said this to me: 'Great king, in acting or causing to act, in mutilating or causing to mutilate, in torturing or causing to torture, in inflicting sorrow or causing to inflict sorrow, in oppressing or causing to oppress, in intimidating or causing to intimidate, in taking life, in taking what is not given, in breaking into houses, in plundering, in highway robbery, in committing adultery, in speaking falsehood, in acting, no evil is done.

If with a razor-sharp wheel one were to make the living beings on this earth into one mass of flesh, into one heap of flesh, there would be no evil resulting from that, no coming of evil.

If one were to go along the south bank of the Ganges killing, slaughtering, mutilating, causing to mutilate, torturing, causing to torture, there would be no evil resulting from that, no coming of evil.

If one were to go along the north bank of the Ganges giving, causing to give, sacrificing, causing to sacrifice, there would be no merit resulting from that, no coming of merit.

By giving, self-control, restraint and truthfulness there is no merit, there is no coming of merit.'

Thus, venerable sir, when I asked Pūraṇa Kassapa about the visible fruit of the ascetic life, he explained the inefficacy of action.

Just as, venerable sir, if asked about a mango, one would speak about a breadfruit, or if asked about a breadfruit, one would speak about a mango; even so, venerable sir, when I asked Pūraṇa Kassapa about the visible fruit of the ascetic life, he explained the inefficacy of action.

Then it occurred to me, venerable sir: 'How could one like me think of disparaging a śramaṇa or a brāhmaṇa living in my territory?'

So I, venerable sir, neither rejoiced at Pūraṇa Kassapa's words nor did I reject them.

Without rejoicing, without rejecting, displeased, without expressing my displeasure, holding back that speech, not overturning it, not overturning it (it would be).

kaṃ.

ka.

) Rising from my seat, I departed, I departed (sī.

syā.

kaṃ.

pī.).
166.‘‘Karoto kho, mahārāja, kārayato’’tiādīsu karototi sahatthā karontassa. Kārayatoti āṇattiyā kārentassa. Chindatoti paresaṃ hatthādīni chindantassa. Pacatoti pare daṇḍena pīḷentassa. Socayatoti parassa bhaṇḍaharaṇādīhi socayato. Socāpayatoti sokaṃ sayaṃ karontassapi parehi kārāpentassapi . Kilamatoti āhārupacchedabandhanāgārappavesanādīhi sayaṃ kilamantassapi parehi kilamāpentassapi. Phandato phandāpayatoti paraṃ phandantaṃ phandanakāle sayampi phandato parampi phandāpayato. Pāṇamatipātāpayatoti pāṇaṃ hanantassapi hanāpentassapi. Evaṃ sabbattha karaṇakāraṇavaseneva attho veditabbo. Sandhinti gharasandhiṃ. Nillopanti mahāvilopaṃ. Ekāgārikanti ekameva gharaṃ parivāretvā viluppanaṃ. Paripantheti āgatāgatānaṃ acchindanatthaṃ magge tiṭṭhato. Karoto na karīyati pāpanti yaṃ kiñci pāpaṃ karomīti saññāya karotopi pāpaṃ na karīyati, natthi pāpaṃ. Sattā pana pāpaṃ karomāti evaṃsaññino hontīti dīpeti. Khurapariyantenāti khuraneminā, khuradhārasadisapariyantena vā. Ekaṃ maṃsakhalanti ekaṃ maṃsarāsiṃ. Puñjanti tasseva vevacanaṃ. Tatonidānanti ekamaṃsakhalakaraṇanidānaṃ. Dakkhiṇanti dakkhiṇatīre manussā kakkhaḷā dāruṇā, te sandhāya ‘‘hananto’’tiādimāha. Uttaratīre sattā saddhā honti pasannā buddhamāmakā dhammamāmakā saṅghamāmakā, te sandhāya dadantotiādimāha. Tattha yajantoti mahāyāgaṃ karonto. Damenāti indriyadamena uposathakammena vā. Saṃyamenāti sīlasaṃyamena. Saccavajjenāti saccavacanena. Āgamoti āgamanaṃ, pavattīti attho. Sabbathāpi pāpapuññānaṃ kiriyameva paṭikkhipati. Ambaṃ puṭṭho labujaṃ byākaroti nāma, yo kīdiso ambo kīdisāni vā ambassa khandhapaṇṇapupphaphalānīti vutte ediso labujo edisāni vā labujassa khandhapaṇṇapupphaphalānīti byākaroti. Vijiteti āṇāpavattidese. Apasādetabbanti viheṭhetabbaṃ. Anabhinanditvāti ‘‘sādhu sādhū’’ti evaṃ pasaṃsaṃ akatvā. Appaṭikkositvāti bāladubbhāsitaṃ tayā bhāsitanti evaṃ appaṭibāhitvā. Anuggaṇhantoti sārato aggaṇhanto. Anikkujjantoti sāravaseneva idaṃ nissaraṇaṃ, ayaṃ paramatthoti hadaye aṭṭhapento. Byañjanaṃ pana tena uggahitañceva nikkujjitañca.
166.
"’Doing, indeed, great king, causing to do,’” in these and other instances, "doing" means doing with one's own hand.
"Causing to do" means causing (someone) to do through command.
"Cutting off" means cutting off the hands and other (limbs) of others.
"Tormenting" means tormenting others with a stick.
"Grieving" means causing grief to another through the taking away of goods and other things.
"Causing to grieve" means oneself doing sorrow, and causing others to do (it) as well.
"Fatiguing" means oneself becoming exhausted by the cutting off of food, imprisonment, entering a house, and other things, and causing others to become exhausted as well.
"Shaking, causing to shake" means shaking another person, and at the time of shaking, oneself also shaking, and causing another to shake as well.
"Causing to destroy life" means oneself killing a living being, and causing (another) to kill as well.
In this way, the meaning should be understood everywhere according to the basis of cause and effect.
Sandhi means house-breaking.
Nillopa means total destruction.
Ekāgārika means plundering after surrounding just one house.
Paripantha means standing in the road for the purpose of intercepting those coming and going.
"Doing, evil is not done," is when, with the thought, "I am doing some evil," even doing, evil is not done, there is no evil.
"Beings have the idea, ‘We are doing evil,’" this he shows.
Khurapariyantena means with a razor’s edge, or with an edge similar to a razor’s edge.
Ekaṃ maṃsakhalanti means a single mass of meat.
Puñjanti is a synonym of that itself.
Tatonidānaṃ means having as its origin a single mass of meat.
Dakkhiṇaṃ means on the southern bank the people are rough and cruel; referring to them, he says, "killing," and so on.
On the northern bank, beings are faithful, pleased, regarding the Buddha as their own, regarding the Dharma as their own, regarding the Saṃgha as their own; referring to them, he says, "giving," and so on.
Tattha yajanti means performing a great sacrifice (mahāyāgaṃ).
Damena means by the restraint of the senses (indriya-damena), or by the uposatha observance.
Saṃyamena means by the restraint of morality (śīla).
Saccavajjenāti means by truthful speech.
Āgamo means arrival; pavatti means outcome.
In every way, he rejects the doing of evil and also of merit (puṇya).
Asked about a mango (amba), he explains about a breadfruit (labuja), namely, when asked, "What sort of thing is a mango, what sort of things are the trunk, leaves, flowers, and fruits of a mango?" he explains, "This sort of thing is a breadfruit, these sorts of things are the trunk, leaves, flowers, and fruits of a breadfruit."
Vijiteti means in a place where his command is carried out.
Apasādetabbaṃ means should be injured.
Anabhinanditvā means without doing praise saying, "Good, good," in this way.
Appaṭikkositvā means without rejecting in this way, "That which was spoken by you is foolish ill-speaking."
Anuggaṇhanto means not taking the essence.
Anikkujjanto means establishing in the heart, "This is the release, this is the ultimate meaning" only through the force of the essence.
However, the expression (byañjana) is both taken up by him and rejected.
167
167. ‘‘Ekamidāhaṃ, bhante, samayaṃ yena makkhali gosālo tenupasaṅkamiṃ; upasaṅkamitvā makkhalinā gosālena saddhiṃ sammodiṃ. Sammodanīyaṃ kathaṃ sāraṇīyaṃ vītisāretvā ekamantaṃ nisīdiṃ. Ekamantaṃ nisinno kho ahaṃ, bhante, makkhaliṃ gosālaṃ etadavocaṃ – ‘yathā nu kho imāni, bho gosāla, puthusippāyatanāni…pe… sakkā nu kho, bho gosāla, evameva diṭṭheva dhamme sandiṭṭhikaṃ sāmaññaphalaṃ paññapetu’nti?
“On one occasion, venerable sir, I approached Makkhali Gosāla; having approached Makkhali Gosāla, I exchanged greetings with him.

After exchanging courteous and amiable talk, I sat down to one side.

Having sat down to one side, venerable sir, I said to Makkhali Gosāla: ‘Just as there are these various crafts and occupations… is it possible, venerable Gosāla, in just the same way to explain a fruit of the ascetic life visible in this very life?’
167-169. Makkhalivāde paccayoti hetuvevacanameva, ubhayenāpi vijjamānameva kāyaduccaritādīnaṃ saṃkilesapaccayaṃ, kāyasucaritādīnañca visuddhipaccayaṃ paṭikkhipati. Attakāreti attakāro. Yena attanā katakammena ime sattā devattampi mārattampi brahmattampi sāvakabodhimpi paccekabodhimpi sabbaññutampi pāpuṇanti, tampi paṭikkhipati. Dutiyapadena yaṃ parakāraṃ parassa ovādānusāsaniṃ nissāya ṭhapetvā mahāsattaṃ avaseso jano manussasobhagyataṃ ādiṃ katvā yāva arahattaṃ pāpuṇāti, taṃ parakāraṃ paṭikkhipati. Evamayaṃ bālo jinacakke pahāraṃ deti nāma. Natthi purisakāreti yena purisakārena sattā vuttappakārā sampattiyo pāpuṇanti , tampi paṭikkhipati. Natthi balanti yamhi attano bale patiṭṭhitā sattā vīriyaṃ katvā tā sampattiyo pāpuṇanti, taṃ balaṃ paṭikkhipati. Natthi vīriyantiādīni sabbāni purisakāravevacanāneva. ‘‘Idaṃ no vīriyena idaṃ purisathāmena, idaṃ purisaparakkamena pavatta’’nti evaṃ pavattavacanapaṭikkhepakaraṇavasena panetāni visuṃ ādiyanti. Sabbe sattāti oṭṭhagoṇagadrabhādayo anavasese pariggaṇhāti. Sabbe pāṇāti ekindriyo pāṇo, dvindriyo pāṇotiādivasena vadati. Sabbe bhūtāti aṇḍakosavatthikosesu bhūte sandhāya vadati. Sabbe jīvāti sāliyavagodhumādayo sandhāya vadati. Tesu hi so virūhanabhāvena jīvasaññī. Avasā abalā avīriyāti tesaṃ attano vaso vā balaṃ vā vīriyaṃ vā natthi. Niyatisaṅgatibhāvapariṇatāti ettha niyatīti niyatā. Saṅgatīti channaṃ abhijātīnaṃ tattha tattha gamanaṃ. Bhāvoti sabhāvoyeva. Evaṃ niyatiyā ca saṅgatiyā ca bhāvena ca pariṇatā nānappakārataṃ pattā. Yena hi yathā bhavitabbaṃ, so tatheva bhavati. Yena na bhavitabbaṃ, so na bhavatīti dasseti. Chasvevābhijātīsūti chasu eva abhijātīsu ṭhatvā sukhañca dukkhañca paṭisaṃvedenti. Aññā sukhadukkhabhūmi natthīti dasseti. Yonipamukhasatasahassānīti pamukhayonīnaṃ uttamayonīnaṃ cuddasasatasahassāni aññāni ca saṭṭhisatāni aññāni ca chasatāni. Pañca ca kammunosatānīti pañcakammasatāni ca. Kevalaṃ takkamattakena niratthakaṃ diṭṭhiṃ dīpeti. Pañca ca kammāni tīṇi ca kammānītiādīsupi eseva nayo. Keci panāhu – ‘‘pañca ca kammānīti pañcindriyavasena bhaṇati. Tīṇīti kāyakammādivasenā’’ti. Kamme ca upaḍḍhakamme cāti ettha panassa kāyakammañca vacīkammañca kammanti laddhi, manokammaṃ upaḍḍhakammanti. Dvaṭṭhipaṭipadāti dvāsaṭṭhi paṭipadāti vadati. Dvaṭṭhantarakappāti ekasmiṃ kappe catusaṭṭhi antarakappā nāma honti. Ayaṃ pana aññe dve ajānanto evamāha. Chaḷābhijātiyoti kaṇhābhijāti, nīlābhijāti, lohitābhijāti, haliddābhijāti, sukkābhijāti, paramasukkābhijātīti imā cha abhijātiyo vadati. Tattha orabbhikā, sākuṇikā, māgavikā, sūkarikā, luddā, macchaghātakā corā, coraghātakā, bandhanāgārikā, ye vā panaññepi keci kurūrakammantā, ayaṃ kaṇhābhijātīti (a. ni. 6.57) vadati. Bhikkhū nīlābhijātīti vadati, te kira catūsu paccayesu kaṇṭake pakkhipitvā khādanti. ‘‘Bhikkhū kaṇṭakavuttikā’’ti (a. ni. 6.57) ayañhissa pāḷiyeva. Atha vā kaṇṭakavuttikā eva nāma eke pabbajitāti vadati. Lohitābhijāti nāma nigaṇṭhā ekasāṭakāti vadati. Ime kira purimehi dvīhi paṇḍaratarā. Gihī odātavasanā acelakasāvakā haliddābhijātīti vadati. Evaṃ attano paccayadāyake nigaṇṭhehipi jeṭṭhakatare karoti. Ājīvakā ājīvakiniyo sukkābhijātīti vadati. Te kira purimehi catūhi paṇḍaratarā. Nando, vaccho, kiso, saṅkiccho, makkhaligosālo, paramasukkābhijātīti (a. ni. 6.57) vadati. Te kira sabbehi paṇḍaratarā. Aṭṭha purisabhūmiyoti mandabhūmi, khiḍḍābhūmi, padavīmaṃsabhūmi, ujugatabhūmi, sekkhabhūmi, samaṇabhūmi , jinabhūmi, pannabhūmīti imā aṭṭha purisabhūmiyoti vadati. Tattha jātadivasato paṭṭhāya sattadivase sambādhaṭṭhānato nikkhantattā sattā mandā honti momūhā, ayaṃ mandabhūmīti vadati. Ye pana duggatito āgatā honti, te abhiṇhaṃ rodanti ceva viravanti ca, sugatito āgatā taṃ anussaritvā hasanti, ayaṃ khiḍḍābhūmi nāma. Mātāpitūnaṃ hatthaṃ vā pādaṃ vā mañcaṃ vā pīṭhaṃ vā gahetvā bhūmiyaṃ padanikkhipanaṃ padavīmaṃsabhūmi nāma. Padasā gantuṃ samatthakāle ujugatabhūmi nāma. Sippāni sikkhitakāle sekkhabhūmi nāma. Gharā nikkhamma pabbajitakāle samaṇabhūmi nāma. Ācariyaṃ sevitvā jānanakāle jinabhūmi nāma. Bhikkhu ca pannako jino na kiñci āhāti evaṃ alābhiṃ samaṇaṃ pannabhūmīti vadati. Ekūnapaññāsa ājīvakasateti ekūnapaññāsaājīvakavuttisatāni. Paribbājakasateti paribbājakapabbajjāsatāni. Nāgāvāsasateti nāgamaṇḍalasatāni. Vīse indriyasateti vīsatindriyasatāni. Tiṃse nirayasateti tiṃsa nirayasatāni. Rajodhātuyoti rajaokiraṇaṭṭhānāni, hatthapiṭṭhipādapiṭṭhādīni sandhāya vadati. Satta saññīgabbhāti oṭṭhagoṇagadrabhaajapasumigamahiṃse sandhāya vadati. Satta asaññīgabbhāti sālivīhiyavagodhūmakaṅguvarakakudrūsake sandhāya vadati. Nigaṇṭhigabbhāti gaṇṭhimhi jātagabbhā, ucchuveḷunaḷādayo sandhāya vadati. Satta devāti bahū devā. So pana sattāti vadati. Manussāpi anantā, so sattāti vadati. Sattapisācāti pisācā mahantamahantā sattāti vadati. Sarāti mahāsarā, kaṇṇamuṇḍarathakāraanotattasīhappapātachaddantamandākinīkuṇāladahe gahetvā vadati. Pavuṭāti gaṇṭhikā. Papātāti mahāpapātā. Papātasatānīti khuddakapapātasatāni. Supināti mahāsupinā. Supinasatānīti khuddakasupinasatāni. Mahākappinoti mahākappānaṃ. Tattha ekamhā mahāsarā vassasate vassasate kusaggena ekaṃ udakabinduṃ nīharitvā sattakkhattuṃ tamhi sare nirudake kate eko mahākappoti vadati. Evarūpānaṃ mahākappānaṃ caturāsītisatasahassāni khepetvā bāle ca paṇḍite ca dukkhassantaṃ karontīti ayamassa laddhi. Paṇḍitopi kira antarā visujjhituṃ na sakkoti. Bālopi tato uddhaṃ na gacchati. Sīlenāti acelakasīlena vā aññena vā yena kenaci. Vatenāti tādiseneva vatena. Tapenāti tapokammena. Aparipakkaṃ paripāceti nāma, yo ‘‘ahaṃ paṇḍito’’ti antarā visujjhati. Paripakkaṃ phussa phussa byantiṃ karoti nāma yo ‘‘ahaṃ bālo’’ti vuttaparimāṇaṃ kālaṃ atikkamitvā yāti. Hevaṃ natthīti evaṃ natthi. Tañhi ubhayampi na sakkā kātunti dīpeti. Doṇamiteti doṇena mitaṃ viya. Sukhadukkheti sukhadukkhaṃ. Pariyantakateti vuttaparimāṇena kālena katapariyante. Natthihāyanavaḍḍhaneti natthi hāyanavaḍḍhanāni. Na saṃsāro paṇḍitassa hāyati, na bālassa vaḍḍhatīti attho. Ukkaṃsāvakaṃseti ukkaṃsāvakaṃsā. Hāyanavaḍḍhanānametaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Idāni tamatthaṃ upamāya sādhento ‘‘seyyathāpi nāmā’’tiādimāha. Tattha suttaguḷeti veṭhetvā katasuttaguḷe. Nibbeṭhiyamānameva paletīti pabbate vā rukkhagge vā ṭhatvā khittaṃ suttappamāṇena nibbeṭhiyamānameva gacchati, sutte khīṇe tattheva tiṭṭhati, na gacchati. Evameva vuttakālato uddhaṃ na gacchatīti dasseti.
[Garuda Purana 167-169]

In the doctrine of Makkhali, the word paccaya is just a synonym for hetu (cause). With both words, he rejects the real condition for defilement, i.e. wrong bodily conduct, etc., and the real condition for purification, i.e. right bodily conduct, etc.

Attakāra means personal determination.

He rejects also the karma (action) by reason of which beings attain the state of a god (devattaṃ), the state of Māra (mārattaṃ), the state of Brahmā (brahmattampi), the enlightenment of a disciple (sāvakabodhiṃ), the enlightenment of a paccekabuddha (paccekabodhiṃ), or omniscience (sabbaññutaṃ).

By the second expression, he rejects that other-determination (parakāraṃ) through reliance on the exhortation and instruction of another person (parassa ovādānusāsaniṃ nissāya), apart from a Great Being (mahāsattaṃ), the remaining people attain from good fortune in the human state (manussasobhagyataṃ) up to arahatship (arahattaṃ pāpuṇāti).

Thus, this fool strikes a blow at the Wheel of the Conqueror (jinacakke pahāraṃ deti).

"No personal determination" (natthi purisakāreti): he rejects the personal determination (purisakārena) through which beings attain the aforementioned kinds of success (vuttappakārā sampattiyo pāpuṇanti).

“No power” (natthi balanti): he denies that beings can establish themselves upon their own power (attano bale patiṭṭhitā), arouse their energy (vīriyaṃ katvā), and attain those kinds of success (tā sampattiyo pāpuṇanti).

"No energy," etc. are all just synonyms for personal determination (purisakāravevacanāneva).

They are brought in separately in order to reject the claim: "This has occurred through our energy (idaṃ no vīriyena), this through personal strength (purisathāmena), and this through personal fortitude (purisaparakkamena pavatta)."

"All sentient beings" (sabbe sattā): he includes camels, oxen, donkeys, etc., without exception (anavasese pariggaṇhāti).

"All living beings" (sabbe pāṇā): he says this with reference to creatures having one faculty (ekindriyo pāṇo) or two faculties (dvindriyo pāṇo), etc.

"All creatures" (sabbe bhūtā): this refers to beings born from eggs (aṇḍakosa) or from the womb (vatthikosesu bhūte sandhāya vadati).

"All souls" (sabbe jīvā): this refers to rice, barley, wheat, etc. (sāli yava godhumādayo sandhāya vadati).

Because they undergo growth (virūhanabhāvena), he regards them as having souls (jīvasaññī).

"Are helpless (avasā), powerless (abalā), devoid of energy (avīriyā)": they have no self-control (attano vaso), power (balaṃ), or energy (vīriyaṃ).

"Niyatisangatibhāvapariṇatā (destiny, connection, nature and change)": here, niyati means fixed.

“Circumstance (saṅgatīti)": going here and there among the six classes of men (channaṃ abhijātīnaṃ tattha tattha gamanaṃ).

"Nature (bhāvo)": the inner nature itself (sabhāvoyeva).

Thus, through destiny (niyatiyā), circumstance (saṅgatiyā), and nature (bhāvena), they have attained various kinds of change (nānappakārataṃ pattā).

Whatever will be will be (yena hi yathā bhavitabbaṃ), so that is how it is (so tatheva bhavati).

Whatever will not be will not be (yena na bhavitabbaṃ, so na bhavati), this he shows (dasseti).

"The six classes of men" (chasvevābhijātīsūti): abiding in the six classes of men (chasu eva abhijātīsu ṭhatvā), they experience pleasure and pain (sukhañca dukkhañca paṭisaṃvedenti).

He shows that there is no other plane of pleasure and pain (aññā sukhadukkhabhūmi natthi).

“Hundreds of thousands of beginnings of wombs (yonipamukhasatasahassāni)”: fourteen hundred thousand of the main and best wombs (pamukhayonīnaṃ uttamayonīnaṃ cuddasasatasahassāni), plus six hundred others (aññāni ca saṭṭhisatāni) and six hundred others (aññāni ca chasatāni).

"Five hundred kinds of kamma (pañca ca kammunosatāni)" means five hundred kamma-sata (pañcakammasatāni).

He explains a senseless view (niratthakaṃ diṭṭhiṃ dīpeti) devised solely by mere reasoning (kevalaṃ takkamattakena).

The same principle applies in the case of five kinds of kamma (pañca ca kammāni), three kinds of kamma (tīṇi ca kammāni), etc.

But some say: "He speaks of five kinds of kamma (pañca ca kammāni) by way of the five sense faculties (pañcindriyavasena bhaṇati)."

"Three" means by way of bodily kamma, etc. (kāyakammādivasenā).

“Full kamma and half kamma (kamme ca upaḍḍhakamme ca)”: here his theory is that bodily kamma (kāyakammañca) and verbal kamma (vacīkammañca) are full kamma (kammanti laddhi), and mental kamma (manokammaṃ) is half kamma (upaḍḍhakammanti).

“Sixty-two pathways (dvaṭṭhipaṭipadā)” means he speaks of sixty-two pathways (dvāsaṭṭhi paṭipadāti vadati).

"Sixty-two sub-aeons (dvaṭṭhantarakappā)": in a single great aeon (ekasmiṃ kappe) there are sixty-four sub-aeons (catusaṭṭhi antarakappā nāma honti).

But since he does not know about two of these (aññe dve ajānanto), he says thus (evamāha).

He declares that there are six classes of men (chaḷābhijātiyo): the black (kaṇhābhijāti), the blue (nīlābhijāti), the red (lohitābhijāti), the yellow (haliddābhijāti), the white (sukkābhijāti), and the ultimate white (paramasukkābhijāti).

The black class (kaṇhābhijāti) is made up of butchers (orabbhikā), hunters (sākuṇikā), trappers of wild beasts (māgavikā), butchers of pigs (sūkarikā), hunters (luddā), fishermen (macchaghātakā), thieves (corā), executioners (coraghātakā), prison wardens (bandhanāgārikā), and those in other cruel lines of work (ye vā panaññepi keci kurūrakammantā) (A.

N.

6.
57). He says (vadati).

The blue class (nīlābhijāti) is made up of bhikkhus (bhikkhū nīlābhijātīti vadati). For bhikkhus, he says, eat having thrown thorns (kaṇṭake pakkhipitvā khādanti) into the four requisites (catūsu paccayesu).
“The monks have thorny behavior” ( bhikkhū kaṇṭakavuttikā)— (a.
ni.
6.
57) This very thing is indeed the text.
Or alternatively, he says that some who have gone forth are named as having thorny behavior ( kaṇṭakavuttikā eva nāma eke pabbajitāti vadati).
The red class is made up of the one-robed he Nigaṇṭhas ; ( lohitābhijāti nāma nigaṇṭhā ekasāṭakāti vadati).
for these are purer than the former two. ( ime kira purimehi dvīhi paṇḍaratarā).
He says, "Lay followers in white robes are of the yellow class," ( gihī odātavasanā acelakasāvakā haliddābhijātīti vadati)
Thus he makes his own lay supporters superior even to the Nigaṇṭhas. ( evaṃ attano paccayadāyake nigaṇṭhehipi jeṭṭhakatare karoti).
He says, "The Ājīvakas and Ājīvakinīs are of the white class." ( ājīvakā ājīvakiniyo sukkābhijātīti vadati).
for these, he says, are purer than the previous four. ( te kira purimehi catūhi paṇḍaratarā).
The ultimate white class is made up of Nanda Vaccha, Kisa Saṅkiccha, and Makkhali Gosāla ( nando, vaccho, kiso, saṅkiccho, makkhaligosālo, paramasukkābhijātīti) (a.
ni.
6.
57) He says. ( vadati)
for they are the purest of all. ( te kira sabbehi paṇḍaratarā).
He declares that there are eight stages in the life of man: the stage of feebleness (mandabhūmi); the stage of play (khiḍḍābhūmi); the stage of learning to walk (padavīmaṃsabhūmi); the erect stage (ujugatabhūmi); the stage of training (sekkhabhūmi); the recluse stage (samaṇabhūmi); the conqueror stage (jinabhūmi); and the prostrate stage (pannabhūmi). ( aṭṭha purisabhūmiyoti mandabhūmi, khiḍḍābhūmi, padavīmaṃsabhūmi, ujugatabhūmi, sekkhabhūmi, samaṇabhūmi , jinabhūmi, pannabhūmīti imā aṭṭha purisabhūmiyoti vadati).
The stage of feebleness: this lasts for seven days following the day of birth; for after coming out from the womb beings are feeble and dull. He calls this the stage of feebleness ( ayaṃ mandabhūmīti vadati).
The stage of play: those who have come from an evil destination often cry and howl; those who come from a good destination remember it and laugh. This is called the stage of play. ( ayaṃ khiḍḍābhūmi nāma).
The stage of learning to walk: this is the stage when the child takes hold of its parents’ hands or feet, or a bed or chair, and places its feet on the ground. This is called the stage of learning to walk. ( padavīmaṃsabhūmi nāma).
The erect stage: this is the stage when it is able to walk on its feet. ( ujugatabhūmi nāma).
The stage of training: this is the stage when one has been trained in a craft. ( sekkhabhūmi nāma).
The recluse stage: this is the time when one has renounced the household life and gone forth. ( samaṇabhūmi nāma).
The conqueror stage: this is the time when, having served a teacher, one knows. ( jinabhūmi nāma).
The bhikṣu, wise, victorious, says nothing; thus the ascetic does not obtain the stage of wisdom (pannabhūmīti vadati).
Forty-nine hundreds of Ājīvakas (ekūnapaññāsa ājīvakasateti)—[that is,] forty-nine hundred Ājīvaka means of subsistence (ekūnapaññāsaājīvakavuttisatāni).
Hundreds of wanderers (paribbājakasateti)—[that is,] hundreds of the wanderers’ going forth (paribbājakapabbajjāsatāni).
Hundreds of abodes of nāgas (nāgāvāsasateti)—[that is,] hundreds of circles of nāgas (nāgamaṇḍalasatāni).
Twenty hundreds of faculties (vīse indriyasateti)—[that is,] twenty hundred faculties (vīsatindriyasatāni).
Thirty hundreds of hells (tiṃse nirayasateti)—[that is,] thirty hundreds of hells (tiṃsa nirayasatāni).
"Thirty-six realms of dust": places where dust accumulates; he says this referring to the backs of the hands, bottom of the feet, etc. (rajodhātuyoti rajaokiraṇaṭṭhānāni, hatthapiṭṭhipādapiṭṭhādīni sandhāya vadati).
“Seven spheres of percipient beings”: he says this referring to camels, oxen, donkeys, goats, cattle, deer, and buffaloes. ( satta saññīgabbhāti oṭṭhagoṇagadrabhaajapasumigamahiṃse sandhāya vadati).
“Seven spheres of non-percipient beings”: he says this referring to rice, paddy, barley, wheat, millet, beans, and kudrūsaka. (satta asaññīgabbhāti sālivīhiyavagodhūmakaṅguvarakakudrūsake sandhāya vadati).
“Seven kinds of jointed plants”: plants grown from joints; he refers to sugarcane, bamboo, reeds, etc. (nigaṇṭhigabbhāti gaṇṭhimhi jātagabbhā, ucchuveḷunaḷādayo sandhāya vadati).
“Seven kinds of gods”: there are many kinds of gods, (satta devāti bahū devā).
but he says there are seven (so pana sattāti vadati).
Human beings, too, are of infinite kinds, but he says there are seven (manussāpi anantā, so sattāti vadati).
“Seven kinds of demons”: there are numerous kinds of demons, but he says there are seven. (sattapisācāti pisācā mahantamahantā sattāti vadati).
“Seven great lakes”: he says this mentioning the Kaṇṇamuṇḍa, Rathakāra, Anotatta, Sìhappapāta, Chaddanta, Mandākinī, and Kuṇāladaha. (sarāti mahāsarā, kaṇṇamuṇḍarathakāraanotattasīhappapātachaddantamandākinīkuṇāladahe gahetvā vadati).
The toggle is allowable. (pavuṭāti gaṇṭhikā).
papātāti mahāpapātā.
It falls; it is a great fall.

papātasatānīti khuddakapapātasatāni.
Hundreds of falls; it is a small hundred of falls.

supināti mahāsupinā.
It dreams; it is a great dream.

supinasatānīti khuddakasupinasatāni.
Hundreds of dreams; it is a small hundred of dreams.

mahākappinoti mahākappānaṃ.
Of a great aeon; it is of great aeons.

tattha ekamhā mahāsarā vassasate vassasate kusaggena ekaṃ udakabinduṃ nīharitvā sattakkhattuṃ tamhi sare nirudake kate eko mahākappoti vadati.
There, he describes a great aeon as the time it would take to drain a single great lake seven times by removing a single drop of water with the tip of a blade of kusa-grass once every hundred years.

evarūpānaṃ mahākappānaṃ caturāsītisatasahassāni khepetvā bāle ca paṇḍite ca dukkhassantaṃ karontīti ayamassa laddhi.
His theory asserts that when eighty-four hundred thousand of such great aeons have passed, the foolish (bāle) and the wise (paṇḍite) make an end to suffering (duḥkhassāntaṃ).

paṇḍitopi kira antarā visujjhituṃ na sakkoti.
The wise man, he says, cannot purify himself before this.

bālopi tato uddhaṃ na gacchati.
and the fool does not continue on beyond.

sīlenāti acelakasīlena vā aññena vā yena kenaci.
By this moral discipline of the naked ascetics or by any other.

vatenāti tādiseneva vatena.
“Observance” should be understood similarly.

tapenāti tapokammena.
By austerity, it is through deeds of asceticism.

aparipakkaṃ paripāceti nāma, yo ‘‘ahaṃ paṇḍito’’ti antarā visujjhati.
That the one who considers himself a wise man should “ripen unripened kamma” i.e. that he should purify himself beforehand,

paripakkaṃ phussa phussa byantiṃ karoti nāma yo ‘‘ahaṃ bālo’’ti vuttaparimāṇaṃ kālaṃ atikkamitvā yāti.
or “eliminate ripened kamma whenever it comes up,” or that the one who considers himself a fool should continue on beyond the time stated to be the limits —

hevaṃ natthīti evaṃ natthi.
“that cannot be,”

tañhi ubhayampi na sakkā kātunti dīpeti.
i.e. neither is able to do that.

doṇamiteti doṇena mitaṃ viya.
Measured by a doṇa; it is as if measured by a doṇa.

sukhadukkheti sukhadukkhaṃ.
Pleasure and pain; it is pleasure and pain.

pariyantakateti vuttaparimāṇena kālena katapariyante.
With a limit made; it is with a limit made by the stated measure of time.

natthihāyanavaḍḍhaneti natthi hāyanavaḍḍhanāni.
There is no decrease or increase; there are no decreases or increases.

na saṃsāro paṇḍitassa hāyati, na bālassa vaḍḍhatīti attho.
“Saṃsāra’s limits … . can neither be shortened nor extended”: saṃsāra is not shortened for the wise man (paṇḍitassa), nor extended for the fool (bālassa).

ukkaṃsāvakaṃseti ukkaṃsāvakaṃsā.
Superiority and inferiority; they are superiorities and inferiorities.

hāyanavaḍḍhanānametaṃ adhivacanaṃ.
This is a designation for decrease and increase.

idāni tamatthaṃ upamāya sādhento ‘‘seyyathāpi nāmā’’tiādimāha.
Now, to demonstrate that meaning with a simile, he said, "Just as, for example..." and so forth.

tattha suttaguḷeti veṭhetvā katasuttaguḷe.
There, a ball of thread; it is a ball of thread made by wrapping [it].

nibbeṭhiyamānameva paletīti pabbate vā rukkhagge vā ṭhatvā khittaṃ suttappamāṇena nibbeṭhiyamānameva gacchati, sutte khīṇe tattheva tiṭṭhati, na gacchati.
Just as it unrolls, it flees; having stood on a mountain or at the top of a tree, something thrown unrolls as it goes according to the thread's measure, and when the thread is exhausted, it stands right there and does not go [further].

evameva vuttakālato uddhaṃ na gacchatīti dasseti.
Just so, he shows that [one] does not go beyond the stated time.
168
168. ‘‘Evaṃ vutte, bhante, makkhali gosālo maṃ etadavoca – ‘natthi mahārāja hetu natthi paccayo sattānaṃ saṃkilesāya, ahetū ahetu (katthaci) apaccayā sattā saṃkilissanti. Natthi hetu, natthi paccayo sattānaṃ visuddhiyā, ahetū apaccayā sattā visujjhanti. Natthi attakāre, natthi parakāre, natthi purisakāre, natthi balaṃ, natthi vīriyaṃ, natthi purisathāmo, natthi purisaparakkamo . Sabbe sattā sabbe pāṇā sabbe bhūtā sabbe jīvā avasā abalā avīriyā niyatisaṅgatibhāvapariṇatā chasvevābhijātīsu sukhadukkhaṃ sukhañca dukkhañca (syā.) paṭisaṃvedenti. Cuddasa kho panimāni yonipamukhasatasahassāni saṭṭhi ca satāni cha ca satāni pañca ca kammuno satāni pañca ca kammāni tīṇi ca kammāni kamme ca aḍḍhakamme ca dvaṭṭhipaṭipadā dvaṭṭhantarakappā chaḷābhijātiyo aṭṭha purisabhūmiyo ekūnapaññāsa ājīvakasate ekūnapaññāsa paribbājakasate ekūnapaññāsa nāgāvāsasate vīse indriyasate tiṃse nirayasate chattiṃsa rajodhātuyo satta saññīgabbhā satta asaññīgabbhā satta nigaṇṭhigabbhā satta devā satta mānusā satta pisācā satta sarā satta pavuṭā sapuṭā (ka.), pabuṭā (sī.) satta pavuṭasatāni satta papātā satta papātasatāni satta supinā satta supinasatāni cullāsīti mahākappino mahākappuno (ka. sī. pī.) satasahassāni, yāni bāle ca paṇḍite ca sandhāvitvā saṃsaritvā dukkhassantaṃ karissanti. Tattha natthi ‘‘imināhaṃ sīlena vā vatena vā tapena vā brahmacariyena vā aparipakkaṃ vā kammaṃ paripācessāmi, paripakkaṃ vā kammaṃ phussa phussa byantiṃ karissāmī’ti hevaṃ natthi. Doṇamite sukhadukkhe pariyantakate saṃsāre , natthi hāyanavaḍḍhane, natthi ukkaṃsāvakaṃse. Seyyathāpi nāma suttaguḷe khitte nibbeṭhiyamānameva paleti, evameva bāle ca paṇḍite ca sandhāvitvā saṃsaritvā dukkhassantaṃ karissantī’ti.
168. “When this had been said, venerable sir, Makkhali Gosāla said this to me: ‘Great king, there is no cause ( hetu ) or condition ( paccaya ) for the defilement ( saṃkilesa ) of beings; beings are defiled without cause or condition.

There is no cause or condition for the purification ( visuddhi ) of beings; beings are purified without cause or condition.

There is no self-determination ( attakāre ), no determination by others ( parakāre ), no human determination ( purisakāre ). There is no power ( balaṃ ), no energy ( vīriyaṃ ), no human strength ( purisathāmo ), no human endeavor (purisaparakkamo ).

All beings ( sabbe sattā ), all living things ( sabbe pāṇā ), all creatures ( sabbe bhūtā ), all souls ( sabbe jīvā ) are powerless ( avasā ), devoid of strength ( abalā ), devoid of effort ( avīriyā ); subject to the changes of fate ( niyati ), circumstance ( saṅgati ), and nature ( bhāva ), they experience pleasure and pain in the six classes of birth ( chasvevābhijātīsu sukhadukkhaṃ ).

There are fourteen hundred thousand principal kinds of generation, and sixty hundred kinds, and six hundred kinds; there are five hundred kinds of action ( kamma ), and five kinds of action, and three kinds of action, and action and half-action; there are sixty-two pathways ( dvaṭṭhipaṭipadā ), sixty-two sub-aeons ( dvaṭṭhantarakappā ), six classes of men ( chaḷābhijātiyo ), eight stages in the life of man ( aṭṭha purisabhūmiyo ), forty-nine hundred modes of livelihood ( ekūnapaññāsa ājīvakasate ), forty-nine hundred kinds of wanderers ( ekūnapaññāsa paribbājakasate ), forty-nine hundred abodes of Nāgas ( ekūnapaññāsa nāgāvāsasate ), two thousand faculties ( vīse indriyasate ), three thousand hells ( tiṃse nirayasate ), thirty-six realms of rajodhātuyo, seven sentient beings in the womb ( satta saññīgabbhā ), seven non-sentient beings in the womb ( satta asaññīgabbhā ), seven nigaṇṭhi beings in the womb ( satta nigaṇṭhigabbhā ), seven gods ( satta devā ), seven humans ( satta mānusā ), seven pisācas ( satta pisācā ), seven saras ( satta sarā ), seven pavuṭas ( satta pavuṭā ), seven hundred pavuṭas ( satta pavuṭasatāni ), seven chasms ( satta papātā ), seven hundred chasms ( satta papātasatāni ), seven dreams ( satta supinā ), seven hundred dreams ( satta supinasatāni ), eighty-four hundred thousand great aeons ( cullāsīti mahākappino mahākappuno satasahassāni ), through which fools and the wise, running and wandering, will make an end to suffering ( dukkhassantaṃ karissanti ).

There is none of this: “By this virtue ( sīlena ) or observance ( vatena ) or asceticism ( tapena ) or holy life ( brahmacariyena ) I shall make unripened action ( kamma ) ripen or annihilate ripened action as it comes."

Pleasure ( sukha ) and pain ( dukkha ) are measured out. The round of rebirths ( saṃsāre ) is limited, there is no shortening or extending it, no increasing or decreasing it.

Just as a ball of string when thrown goes as far as the string unwinds, so too, by running and wandering through the round of rebirths, fools and the wise both will make an end to suffering.’
167-169. Makkhalivāde paccayoti hetuvevacanameva, ubhayenāpi vijjamānameva kāyaduccaritādīnaṃ saṃkilesapaccayaṃ, kāyasucaritādīnañca visuddhipaccayaṃ paṭikkhipati. Attakāreti attakāro.
