246-247. "Wandering along the street" in the simile of the divine eye means repeatedly wandering.

Alternatively, the reading could be vīthiṃ carantetipi.

This is the meaning.

There, in the middle of the city, the upper-terraced building (pāsāda) in the central square (siṅghāṭaka) is to be seen as like the material body (karajakāya) of this bhikkhu. The man with keen sight (cakkhumā puriso) standing in the building is like the bhikkhu who has attained the divine eye (dibbacakkhuṃ). Those entering a house (gehaṃ pavisantā) are like those entering the mother’s womb (mātukucchiyaṃ) by way of relinking (paṭisandhivasena); those leaving the house (gehā nikkhamantā) are like those leaving the womb (mātukucchito nikkhamantā); those wandering along the streets (rathikāya vīthiṃ sañcarantā) are like those beings (sattā) who repeatedly wander in saṃsāra (aparāparaṃ sañcaraṇakasattā); those sitting in front, in the open air (abbhokāsaṭṭhāne) in the central square (majjhe siṅghāṭake), are like the beings born in the three realms (tīsu bhavesu tattha tattha nibbattasattā); the time of appearance (āvibhūtakālo) of those people to the man standing at the foot of the building (pāsādatale ṭhitapurisassa tesaṃ manussānaṃ) is like the time of appearance (āvibhūtakālo) of beings born in the three realms (tīsu bhavesu nibbattasattānaṃ) to the bhikkhu who, having directed his mind (cittaṃ abhinīharitvā) to the knowledge of the divine eye (dibbacakkhuñāṇāya), is sitting.

This statement is made for ease of teaching (desanāsukhatthameva vuttaṃ).

But the immaterial realm (āruppe) does not come into the range (gocaro) of the divine eye (dibbacakkhussa).
248
248. ‘‘So evaṃ samāhite citte parisuddhe pariyodāte anaṅgaṇe vigatūpakkilese mudubhūte kammaniye ṭhite āneñjappatte āsavānaṃ khayañāṇāya cittaṃ abhinīharati abhininnāmeti. So idaṃ dukkhanti yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti , ayaṃ dukkhasamudayoti yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti, ayaṃ dukkhanirodhoti yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti, ayaṃ dukkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadāti yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti. Ime āsavāti yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti, ayaṃ āsavasamudayoti yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti, ayaṃ āsavanirodhoti yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti, ayaṃ āsavanirodhagāminī paṭipadāti yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti. Tassa evaṃ jānato evaṃ passato kāmāsavāpi cittaṃ vimuccati, bhavāsavāpi cittaṃ vimuccati, avijjāsavāpi cittaṃ vimuccati, ‘vimuttasmiṃ vimuttami’ti ñāṇaṃ hoti, ‘khīṇā jāti, vusitaṃ brahmacariyaṃ, kataṃ karaṇīyaṃ, nāparaṃ itthattāyā’ti pajānāti.
248.

"When his mind is thus concentrated (samāhite citte), purified (parısuddhe), bright (pariyodāte), unblemished (anaṅgaṇe), free from defects (vigatūpakkilese), pliant (mudubhūte), workable (kammaniye), steady (ṭhite), and attained to imperturbability (āneñjappatte), he directs and inclines (abhinīharati abhininnāmeti) it to the knowledge of the destruction of the taints (āsavānaṃ khayañāṇāya).

He understands as it really is: "This is suffering (idaṃ dukkham)," he understands as it really is: "This is the origin of suffering (dukkhasamudayo)," he understands as it really is: "This is the cessation of suffering (dukkhanirodho)," he understands as it really is: "This is the path leading to the cessation of suffering (dukkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadā)."

He understands as it really is: "These are the taints (āsavā)," he understands as it really is: "This is the origin of the taints (āsavasamudayo)," he understands as it really is: "This is the cessation of the taints (āsavanirodho)," he understands as it really is: "This is the path leading to the cessation of the taints (āsavanirodhagāminī paṭipadā)."

Knowing and seeing thus (tassa evaṃ jānato evaṃ passato), his mind is liberated from the taint of sensual desire (kāmāsavāpi cittaṃ vimuccati), from the taint of becoming (bhavāsavāpi cittaṃ vimuccati), and from the taint of ignorance (avijjāsavāpi cittaṃ vimuccati). When it is liberated, the knowledge arises: 'It is liberated (vimuttasmiṃ vimuttami).' He understands: 'Destroyed is birth (khīṇā jāti), the holy life has been lived (vusitaṃ brahmacariyaṃ), what had to be done has been done (kataṃ karaṇīyaṃ), there is nothing further beyond this (nāparaṃ itthattāyā).'"
248.So evaṃ samāhite citteti idha vipassanāpādakaṃ catutthajjhānacittaṃ veditabbaṃ. Āsavānaṃ khayañāṇāyāti āsavānaṃ khayañāṇanibbattanatthāya. Ettha ca āsavānaṃ khayo nāma maggopi phalampi nibbānampi bhaṅgopi vuccati. ‘‘Khaye ñāṇaṃ, anuppāde ñāṇa’’nti ettha hi maggo āsavānaṃ khayoti vutto. ‘‘Āsavānaṃ khayā samaṇo hotī’’ti (ma. ni. 1.438) ettha phalaṃ. Ettha nibbānaṃ. ‘‘Āsavānaṃ khayo vayo bhedo aniccatā antaradhāna’’nti ettha bhaṅgo. Idha pana nibbānaṃ adhippetaṃ. Arahattamaggopi vaṭṭatiyeva. Cittaṃabhinīharatīti vipassanā cittaṃ tanninnaṃ tappoṇaṃ tappabbhāraṃ karoti. So idaṃ dukkhantiādīsu ‘‘ettakaṃ dukkhaṃ, na ito bhiyyo’’ti sabbampi dukkhasaccaṃ sarasalakkhaṇapaṭivedhena yathābhūtaṃ pajānātīti attho. Tassa ca dukkhassa nibbattikaṃ taṇhaṃ ‘‘ayaṃ dukkhasamudayo’’ti. Tadubhayampi yaṃ ṭhānaṃ patvā nirujjhati, taṃ tesaṃ appavattiṃ nibbānaṃ ‘‘ayaṃ dukkhanirodho’’ti; tassa ca sampāpakaṃ ariyamaggaṃ ‘‘ayaṃ dukkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadā’’ti sarasalakkhaṇapaṭivedhena yathābhūtaṃ pajānātīti attho. Evaṃ sarūpato saccāni dassetvā puna kilesavasena pariyāyato dassento ‘‘ime āsavā’’tiādimāha. Tassa evaṃ jānato evaṃ passatoti tassa bhikkhuno evaṃ jānantassa evaṃ passantassa, saha vipassanāya koṭippattaṃ maggaṃ kathesi. Kāmāsavāti kāmāsavato. Vimuccatīti iminā maggakkhaṇaṃ dasseti. Vimuttasminti iminā phalakkhaṇaṃ. Vimuttamiti ñāṇaṃ hotīti iminā paccavekkhaṇañāṇaṃ. Khīṇā jātītiādīhi tassa bhūmiṃ. Tena hi ñāṇena khīṇāsavo paccavekkhanto khīṇā jātītiādīni pajānāti. Katamā panassa jāti khīṇā? Kathañca naṃ pajānātīti? Na tāvassa atītā jāti khīṇā, pubbeva khīṇattā. Na anāgatā, anāgate vāyāmābhāvato. Na paccuppannā, vijjamānattā. Yā pana maggassa abhāvitattā uppajjeyya ekacatupañcavokārabhavesu ekacatupañcakkhandhappabhedā jāti, sā maggassa bhāvitattā āyatiṃ anuppādadhammataṃ āpajjanena khīṇā. Taṃ so maggabhāvanāya pahīnakilese paccavekkhitvā ‘‘kilesābhāve vijjamānampi kammaṃ āyatiṃ appaṭisandhikaṃva hotī’’ti jānanto pajānāti. Vusitanti vutthaṃ parivutthaṃ. Brahmacariyanti maggabrahmacariyaṃ. Puthujjanakalyāṇakena hi saddhiṃ satta sekkhā brahmacariyavāsaṃ vasanti nāma, khīṇāsavo vutthavāso, tasmā so attano brahmacariyavāsaṃ paccavekkhanto vusitaṃ brahmacariyanti pajānāti. Kataṃkaraṇīyanti catūsu saccesu catūhi maggehi pariññāpahānasacchikiriyābhāvanāvasena soḷasavidhaṃ kiccaṃ niṭṭhāpitaṃ. Tena tena maggena pahātabbakilesā pahīnā, dukkhamūlaṃ samucchinnanti attho. Puthujjanakalyāṇakādayo hi taṃ kiccaṃ karonti, khīṇāsavo katakaraṇīyo. Tasmā so attano karaṇīyaṃ paccavekkhanto kataṃ karaṇīyanti pajānāti. Nāparaṃ itthattāyāti idāni puna itthabhāvāya evaṃ soḷasakiccabhāvāya kilesakkhayabhāvāya vā kattabbaṃ maggabhāvanākiccaṃ me natthīti pajānāti. Atha vā itthattāyāti itthabhāvato imasmā evaṃ pakārā. Idāni vattamānakhandhasantānā aparaṃ khandhasantānaṃ mayhaṃ natthi. Ime pana pañcakkhandhā pariññātā tiṭṭhanti chinnamūlakā rukkhā viya, te carimakacittanirodhena anupādāno viya jātavedo nibbāyissanti apaṇṇattikabhāvañca gamissantīti pajānāti.
248. When his mind is thus concentrated, here, the mind of the fourth jhāna used as the basis for insight should be understood.
“To the knowledge of the destruction of the cankers ( āsavānaṃ khayañāṇāya )": for the purpose of producing the knowledge of the destruction of the cankers.
And here the destruction of the cankers ( āsavānaṃ khayo ) is called the path ( maggo ), the fruit ( phalaṃ ), Nibbāna ( nibbānaṃ ), and dissolution ( bhaṅgo ).
In the passage, “knowledge of destruction, knowledge of non-arising ( khaye ñāṇaṃ, anuppāde ñāṇaṃ )”, the path ( maggo ) is called the destruction of the cankers ( āsavānaṃ khayo ).
In the passage, “Through the destruction of the cankers one is a recluse ( āsavānaṃ khayā samaṇo hoti )", it is the fruit ( phalaṃ ).
Here, it is Nibbāna ( nibbānaṃ ).
And in the passage, “The destruction of the cankers, their falling away, breakup, impermanence, and disappearance ( āsavānaṃ khayo vayo bhedo aniccatā antaradhāna )”, it is dissolution ( bhaṅgo ).
Here, Nibbāna ( nibbānaṃ ) is intended.
The path of arahatship ( arahattamaggo ) is also appropriate.
“He directs and inclines”: he makes the insight consciousness slant, slide, and slope in that direction.
He understands as it really is “this is suffering” He understands as it really is, by penetration of its specific essential characteristic, the entire truth of suffering thus, “There is this much suffering, and none beyond this.”
And he understands as it really is, by penetration of its specific essential characteristic, the craving which produces that suffering thus, “This is the origin of suffering ( ayaṃ dukkhasamudayo )”;
and the state by the attainment of which both suffering and its origin cease, Nibbāna ( nibbānaṃ ), their non- occurrence, thus, “This is the cessation of suffering ( ayaṃ dukkhanirodho )”; and the noble path ( ariyamaggaṃ ) which brings about its attainment thus, “This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering ( ayaṃ dukkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadā ).”
Having shown the truths in their specific identity, the Buddha speaks the following passage about the cankers to show them again figuratively by way of the defilements: “these are the cankers ( ime āsavā )”.
Knowing and seeing thus, the Buddha explains the path which has reached its peak, together with insight to that bhikkhu knowing thus and seeing thus.
Kāmāsavāti refers to one with sensual influxes.
By the phrase “his mind is liberated ( vimuccati )”, the moment of the path is shown.
By the phrase “when it is liberated ( vimuttasminti )” the moment of the fruit ( phalakkhaṇaṃ ).
And by the phrase “the knowledge arises: It is liberated ( vimuttamiti ñāṇaṃ hoti )” the moment of reviewing knowledge.
By the passage “destroyed is birth ( khīṇā jāti ),” etc., he shows the plane of the reviewing knowledge.
For when the one who has destroyed the cankers reviews with that knowledge, he understands, “Destroyed is birth ( khīṇā jāti ),” etc.
What birth of his is destroyed? And how does he understand it? It is not first and foremost that the past birth has been exhausted, owing to the condition of having been exhausted even before.
It is not a future one, for there is no effort in regard to the future.
And it is not the present one, because that presently exists.
However, whatever birth classified as single aggregate, four and five aggregates in such existences as one, four and five vokāra which would arise owing to the condition of having not developed the right path, that birth has become exhausted by having arrived at the state of the nature of not arising owing to the condition of having developed the right path.
Having reviewed the defilements abandoned by the development of the path, he knows that in the absence of defilements, even though action occurs, it does not bring about relinking in the future.
Vusitaṃ means dwelt, all-round dwelt.
Brahmacariyaṃ means the higher life of the right path.
For the seven learners together with the good worldling are said to be living the holy life, the one with cankers destroyed to have lived the holy life. Therefore, reviewing his own living of the holy life, he understands: “The holy life has been lived.”
“What had to be done has been done”: the sixteen tasks have been completed by way of the full understanding, abandonment, realization and development of the Four Noble Truths by the four paths.
The meaning is that the defilements to be abandoned by each path have been abandoned, and the root of suffering has been eradicated.
The worldling and those of good conduct perform that task, the one with cankers destroyed has done what had to be done.
Therefore, reviewing what had to be done by himself, he understands: “What had to be done has been done.”
“There is nothing further beyond this”: he understands: “Now there is no task of developing the path to be done by me again for this state, that is, for the sixteen tasks or for the destruction of the defilements.”
Or else, “this” can be understood as “beyond this.”
Hence he understands: “Beyond this presently existing continuum of aggregates occurring in such a mode, there is for me no further continuum of aggregates.
These five aggregates (pañcakkhandhā), having been fully understood, remain like trees with their roots cut off. With the cessation of the final consciousness (carimakacittanirodhena), they will be extinguished like a fire without fuel (anupādāno viya jātavedo nibbāyissanti) and will go to a state beyond description (apaṇṇattikabhāvañca gamissanti). Thus, he understands.
249
249. ‘‘Seyyathāpi, mahārāja, pabbatasaṅkhepe udakarahado accho vippasanno anāvilo. Tattha cakkhumā puriso tīre ṭhito passeyya sippisambukampi sakkharakathalampi macchagumbampi carantampi tiṭṭhantampi. Tassa evamassa – ‘ayaṃ kho udakarahado accho vippasanno anāvilo. Tatrime sippisambukāpi sakkharakathalāpi macchagumbāpi carantipi tiṭṭhantipī’ti. Evameva kho, mahārāja, bhikkhu evaṃ samāhite citte parisuddhe pariyodāte anaṅgaṇe vigatūpakkilese mudubhūte kammaniye ṭhite āneñjappatte āsavānaṃ khayañāṇāya cittaṃ abhinīharati abhininnāmeti. ‘So idaṃ dukkha’nti yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti, ‘ayaṃ dukkhasamudayo’ti yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti , ‘ayaṃ dukkhanirodho’ti yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti, ‘ayaṃ dukkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadā’ti yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti. ‘Ime āsavāti yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti, ‘ayaṃ āsavasamudayo’ti yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti, ‘ayaṃ āsavanirodho’ti yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti, ‘ayaṃ āsavanirodhagāminī paṭipadāti yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti. Tassa evaṃ jānato evaṃ passato kāmāsavāpi cittaṃ vimuccati, bhavāsavāpi cittaṃ vimuccati, avijjāsavāpi cittaṃ vimuccati, ‘vimuttasmiṃ vimuttamiti ñāṇaṃ hoti, ‘khīṇā jāti, vusitaṃ brahmacariyaṃ, kataṃ karaṇīyaṃ, nāparaṃ itthattāyā’ti pajānāti. Idaṃ kho, mahārāja, sandiṭṭhikaṃ sāmaññaphalaṃ purimehi sandiṭṭhikehi sāmaññaphalehi abhikkantatarañca paṇītatarañca. Imasmā ca pana, mahārāja, sandiṭṭhikā sāmaññaphalā aññaṃ sandiṭṭhikaṃ sāmaññaphalaṃ uttaritaraṃ vā paṇītataraṃ vā natthī’’ti.
249.

“Just as, great king, in a mountain recess there were a lake with clear water, limpid and undisturbed,

so that a man with good sight standing on the bank could see shells, gravel, and pebbles, and also shoals of fish swimming about and resting.

He would think to himself: ‘This is a lake with clear water, limpid and unsullied.

and there are these shells, gravel, and pebbles, and also these shoals of fish swimming about and resting.’

In the same way, great king, when his mind is thus concentrated, pure, bright, without blemish, rid of defilements, gentle, pliable, steady, and having attained imperturbability, the bhikkhu directs and inclines it to the knowledge of the destruction of the āsavas (cankers, taints, defilements).

‘He understands as it really is: ‘This is suffering’ ( duḥkha), ‘This is the origin of suffering’ ( duḥkha-samudaya), ‘This is the cessation of suffering’ ( duḥkha-nirodha), ‘This is the path leading to the cessation of suffering’ (duḥkha-nirodha-gāminī paṭipadā).’

‘He understands as it really is: ‘These are the āsavas’ , ‘This is the origin of the āsavas’ , ‘This is the cessation of the āsavas’, ‘This is the path leading to the cessation of the āsavas.

Knowing and seeing thus, his mind is liberated from the canker of sensual desire (kāmāsava), from the canker of existence (bhavāsava), and from the canker of ignorance (avijjāsava). When it is liberated, the knowledge arises: ‘It is liberated.’ He understands: ‘Destroyed is birth (jāti), the holy life (brahmacariya) has been lived, what had to be done (karaṇīya) has been done, there is nothing further beyond this.’

This, great king, is a fruit of the homeless life, visible here and now (sandiṭṭhikaṃ sāmaññaphalaṃ), which is more excellent and perfect than the previous fruits.

And, great king, there is no other fruit of the homeless life, visible here and now (sandiṭṭhikaṃ sāmaññaphalaṃ), that is more excellent or perfect than this.”
249.Pabbatasaṅkhepeti pabbatamatthake. Anāviloti nikkaddamo. Sippiyo ca sambukā ca sippisambukaṃ. Sakkharā ca kathalāni ca sakkharakathalaṃ. Macchānaṃ gumbā ghaṭāti macchagumbaṃ. Tiṭṭhantampi carantampīti ettha sakkharakathalaṃ tiṭṭhatiyeva, itarāni carantipi tiṭṭhantipi. Yathā pana antarantarā ṭhitāsupi nisinnāsupi vijjamānāsupi ‘‘etā gāvo carantī’’ti carantiyo upādāya itarāpi carantīti vuccanti. Evaṃ tiṭṭhantameva sakkharakathalaṃ upādāya itarampi dvayaṃ tiṭṭhantanti vuttaṃ. Itarañca dvayaṃ carantaṃ upādāya sakkharakathalampi carantanti vuttaṃ. Tattha cakkhumato purisassa tīre ṭhatvā passato sippikasambukādīnaṃ vibhūtakālo viya āsavānaṃ khayāya cittaṃ abhinīharitvā nisinnassa bhikkhuno catunnaṃ saccānaṃ vibhūtakālo daṭṭhabboti. Ettāvatā vipassanāñāṇaṃ, manomayañāṇaṃ, iddhividhañāṇaṃ, dibbasotañāṇaṃ, cetopariyañāṇaṃ, pubbenivāsañāṇaṃ, dibbacakkhuvasena nipphannaṃ anāgataṃsañāṇayathākammūpagañāṇadvayaṃ, dibbacakkhuñāṇaṃ, āsavakkhayañāṇanti dasa ñāṇāni niddiṭṭhāni honti. Tesaṃ ārammaṇavibhāgo jānitabbo – tattha vipassanāñāṇaṃ parittamahaggataatītānāgatapaccuppannaajjhattabahiddhāvasena sattavidhārammaṇaṃ. Manomayañāṇaṃ nimmitabbarūpāyatanamattameva ārammaṇaṃ karotīti parittapaccuppannabahiddhārammaṇaṃ. Āsavakkhayañāṇaṃ appamāṇabahiddhānavattabbārammaṇaṃ. Avasesānaṃ ārammaṇabhedo visuddhimagge vutto. Uttaritaraṃ vā paṇītataraṃ vāti yena kenaci pariyāyena ito seṭṭhataraṃ sāmaññaphalaṃ nāma natthīti bhagavā arahattanikūṭena desanaṃ niṭṭhāpesi.
249.

Pabbatasaṅkhepeti [means] at the summit of a mountain.

Anāvilo ti [means] without mud.

Sippiyo ca sambukā ca [means] sippisambukaṃ (shells and snails).

Sakkarā ca kathalāni ca [means] sakkarakathalaṃ (gravel and potsherds).

Macchānaṃ gumbā ghaṭāti [means] macchagumbaṃ (a shoal of fish).

"They are standing" and "they are moving": here, the gravel and potsherds are only standing; the others are both moving and standing.

Just as, even when some cows are standing or sitting amidst those that are moving, it is said, "These cows are moving," including those that are moving, the others are also called moving.

Similarly, by including only the standing gravel and potsherds, the other two are also said to be standing.

And by including the other two that are moving, the gravel and potsherds are also said to be moving.

There, the time when the oyster shells and snails, etc., become clear to the man with keen sight standing on the bank seeing them—this is like the time when the Four Noble Truths become clear to the bhikkhu sitting having directed his mind to the knowledge of the destruction of the āsavas (cankers).

At this point, ten kinds of knowledge have been expounded: insight knowledge (vipassanāñāṇaṃ), the knowledge of the mind-made body (manomayañāṇaṃ), the knowledge of the modes of supernormal power (iddhividhañāṇaṃ), the knowledge of the divine ear (dibbasotañāṇaṃ), the knowledge of encompassing the minds of others (cetopariyañāṇaṃ), the knowledge of recollecting past lives (pubbenivāsañāṇaṃ), the pair—the knowledge of the future (anāgataṃsañāṇa) and the knowledge of faring on in accordance with karma (yathākammūpagañāṇa)—accomplished by means of the divine eye (dibbacakkhu), the knowledge of the divine eye (dibbacakkhuñāṇaṃ), and the knowledge of the destruction of the āsavas (āsavakkhayañāṇaṃ).

The analysis of their objects should be known. Therein, insight knowledge (vipassanāñāṇaṃ) has seven kinds of objects: limited (paritta) and exalted (mahaggata), past (atīta), future (anāgata) and present (paccuppanna), internal (ajjhatta) and external (bahiddhā).

The knowledge of the mind-made body (manomayañāṇaṃ) takes as its object only the created form base (nimmitabbarūpāyatana); thus its object is limited (paritta), present (paccuppanna), and external (bahiddhārammaṇaṃ).

The knowledge of the destruction of the āsavas (āsavakkhayañāṇaṃ) has an object which is immeasurable (appamāṇa), external (bahiddhā), and not describable (anavattabba).

For the rest, the division of their objects has been explained in the Visuddhimagga.

And, great king, there is no other fruit of recluseship higher or more sublime than this one. The Buddha concludes the teaching with its culmination in arahatship thus, “There is no fruit of recluseship better in any way than this one.”
250
250. Evaṃ vutte, rājā māgadho ajātasattu vedehiputto bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – ‘‘abhikkantaṃ, bhante, abhikkantaṃ, bhante. Seyyathāpi, bhante, nikkujjitaṃ vā ukkujjeyya, paṭicchannaṃ vā vivareyya, mūḷhassa vā maggaṃ ācikkheyya, andhakāre vā telapajjotaṃ dhāreyya ‘cakkhumanto rūpāni dakkhantī’ti; evamevaṃ, bhante, bhagavatā anekapariyāyena dhammo pakāsito . Esāhaṃ, bhante, bhagavantaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmi dhammañca bhikkhusaṅghañca. Upāsakaṃ maṃ bhagavā dhāretu ajjatagge pāṇupetaṃ saraṇaṃ gataṃ. Accayo maṃ, bhante, accagamā yathābālaṃ yathāmūḷhaṃ yathāakusalaṃ, yohaṃ pitaraṃ dhammikaṃ dhammarājānaṃ issariyakāraṇā jīvitā voropesiṃ. Tassa me, bhante bhagavā accayaṃ accayato paṭiggaṇhātu āyatiṃ saṃvarāyā’’ti.
When this was said, King Ajātaśatru (Ajātasattu), son of Queen Videhi, of Magadha, said this to the Blessed One: “Excellent, venerable sir! Excellent, venerable sir!

Just as, venerable sir, one might set upright what has been overturned, or reveal what has been hidden, or point out the path to one who is lost, or hold up a lamp in the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms, even so has the Dharma (dhamma) been made clear in many ways by the Blessed One (bhagavatā).

I go to the Blessed One (bhagavantaṃ) for refuge (saraṇaṃ), and to the Dharma (dhammañca), and to the Saṅgha (bhikkhusaṅghañca) of monks (bhikkhu).

May the Blessed One (bhagavā) accept me as a lay follower (upāsakaṃ) who has gone for refuge (saraṇaṃ gataṃ) from this day forth, as long as life lasts (pāṇupetaṃ).

Venerable sir, a transgression (accayo) overcame me, as I was foolish (yathābālaṃ), deluded (yathāmūḷhaṃ), and unskilled (yathāakusalaṃ), in that I, for the sake of sovereignty (issariyakāraṇā), took the life (jīvitā voropesiṃ) of my own father, a righteous (dhammikaṃ) and just king (dhammarājānaṃ).

May the Blessed One (bhagavā) accept my confession (accayaṃ) of this fault (accayato), venerable sir, that I may restrain myself (saṃvarāyā) in the future (āyatiṃ."
250. Rājā tattha tattha sādhukāraṃ pavattento ādimajjhapariyosānaṃ sakkaccaṃ sutvā ‘‘ciraṃ vatamhi ime pañhe puthū samaṇabrāhmaṇe pucchanto, thuse koṭṭento viya kiñci sāraṃ nālatthaṃ, aho vata bhagavato guṇasampadā, yo me dīpasahassaṃ jālento viya mahantaṃ ālokaṃ katvā ime pañhe vissajjesi. Suciraṃ vatamhi dasabalassa guṇānubhāvaṃ ajānanto vañcito’’ti cintetvā buddhaguṇānussaraṇasambhūtāya pañcavidhāya pītiyā phuṭasarīro attano pasādaṃ āvikaronto upāsakattaṃ paṭivedesi. Taṃ dassetuṃ ‘‘evaṃ vutte rājā’’tiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha abhikkantaṃ, bhanteti ayaṃ abhikkantasaddo khayasundarābhirūpaabbhanumodanesu dissati. ‘‘Abhikkantā bhante, ratti, nikkhanto paṭhamo yāmo, ciranisinno bhikkhusaṅgho’’tiādīsu (a. ni. 8.20) hi khaye dissati. ‘‘Ayaṃ me puggalo khamati, imesaṃ catunnaṃ puggalānaṃ abhikkantataro ca paṇītataro cā’’tiādīsu (a. ni. 4.100) sundare. Ādīsu abhirūpe. ‘‘Abhikkantaṃ bho, gotamā’’tiādīsu (pārā. 15) abbhanumodane. Idhāpi abbhanumodaneyeva. Yasmā ca abbhanumodane, tasmā ‘sādhu sādhu bhante’ti vuttaṃ hotīti veditabbo. Iminā ca lakkhaṇena idha pasādavasena, pasaṃsāvasena cāyaṃ dvikkhattuṃ vuttoti veditabbo. Athavā abhikkantanti abhikantaṃ atiiṭṭhaṃ atimanāpaṃ atisundaranti vuttaṃ hoti. Ettha ekena abhikkantasaddena desanaṃ thometi, ekena attano pasādaṃ. Ayañhettha adhippāyo, abhikkantaṃ bhante, yadidaṃ bhagavato dhammadesanā, ‘abhikkantaṃ’ yadidaṃ bhagavato dhammadesanaṃ āgamma mama pasādoti. Bhagavatoyeva vā vacanaṃ dve dve atthe sandhāya thometi. Bhagavato vacanaṃ abhikkantaṃ dosanāsanato, abhikkantaṃ guṇādhigamanato. Tathā saddhājananato, paññājananato, sātthato, sabyañjanato, uttānapadato, gambhīratthato, kaṇṇasukhato, hadayaṅgamato, anattukkaṃsanato , aparavambhanato, karuṇāsītalato, paññāvadātato, āpātharamaṇīyato, vimaddakkhamato, suyyamānasukhato, vīmaṃsiyamānahitatoti evamādīhi yojetabbaṃ. Tato parampi catūhi upamāhi desanaṃyeva thometi. Tattha nikkujjitanti adhomukhaṭhapitaṃ heṭṭhāmukhajātaṃ vā. Ukkujjeyyāti upari mukhaṃ kareyya. Paṭicchannanti tiṇapaṇṇādichāditaṃ. Vivareyyāti ugghāṭeyya. Mūḷhassa vāti disāmūḷhassa. Maggaṃ ācikkheyyāti hatthe gahetvā ‘‘esa maggo’’ti vadeyya, andhakāreti kāḷapakkhacātuddasī aḍḍharattaghanavanasaṇḍameghapaṭalehi caturaṅge tame. Ayaṃ tāva anuttānapadattho. Ayaṃ pana sādhippāyayojanā. Yathā koci nikkujjitaṃ ukkujjeyya, evaṃ saddhammavimukhaṃ asaddhamme patitaṃ maṃ asaddhammā vuṭṭhāpentana. Yathā paṭicchannaṃ vivareyya, evaṃ kassapassa bhagavato sāsanantaradhānā pabhuti micchādiṭṭhigahanapaṭicchannaṃ sāsanaṃ vivarantena, yathā mūḷhassa maggaṃ ācikkheyya, evaṃ kummaggamicchāmaggappaṭipannassa me saggamokkhamaggaṃ āvikarontena, yathā andhakāre telapajjotaṃ dhāreyya, evaṃ mohandhakāranimuggassa me buddhādiratanarūpāni apassato tappaṭicchādakamohandhakāraviddhaṃsakadesanāpajjotadhārakena mayhaṃ bhagavatā etehi pariyāyehi pakāsitattā anekapariyāyena dhammo pakāsitoti. Evaṃ desanaṃ thometvā imāya desanāya ratanattaye pasannacitto pasannākāraṃ karonto esāhantiādimāha. Tattha esāhanti eso ahaṃ . Bhagavantaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmīti bhagavā me saraṇaṃ, parāyanaṃ, aghassa tātā, hitassa ca vidhātāti. Iminā adhippāyena bhagavantaṃ gacchāmi bhajāmi sevāmi payirupāsāmi, evaṃ vā jānāmi bujjhāmīti. Yesañhi dhātūnaṃ gatiattho, buddhipi tesaṃ attho. Tasmā gacchāmīti imassa jānāmi bujjhāmīti ayampi attho vutto. Dhammañca bhikkhusaṅghañcāti ettha pana adhigatamagge sacchikatanirodhe yathānusiṭṭhaṃ paṭipajjamāne catūsu apāyesu apatamāne dhāretīti dhammo, so atthato ariyamaggo ceva nibbānañca. Vuttañcetaṃ – ‘‘yāvatā, bhikkhave, dhammā saṅkhatā, ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo tesaṃ aggamakkhāyatī’’ti (a. ni. 4.34) vitthāro. Na kevalañca ariyamaggo ceva nibbānañca. Api ca kho ariyaphalehi saddhiṃ pariyattidhammopi . Vuttañhetaṃ chattamāṇavakavimāne – Ettha hi rāgavirāgoti maggo kathito. Anejamasokanti phalaṃ. Dhammamasaṅkhatanti nibbānaṃ. Appaṭikūlaṃ madhuramimaṃ paguṇaṃ suvibhattanti piṭakattayena vibhattā dhammakkhandhāti. Diṭṭhisīlasaṃghātena saṃhatoti saṅgho, so atthato aṭṭha ariyapuggalasamūho. Vuttañhetaṃ tasmiññeva vimāne – Bhikkhūnaṃ saṅgho bhikkhusaṅgho. Ettāvatā rājā tīṇi saraṇagamanāni paṭivedesi. Idāni tesu saraṇagamanesu kosallatthaṃ saraṇaṃ, saraṇagamanaṃ, yo ca saraṇaṃ gacchati, saraṇagamanappabhedo, saraṇagamanaphalaṃ, saṅkileso, bhedoti, ayaṃ vidhi veditabbo. Seyyathidaṃ – saraṇatthato tāva hiṃsatīti saraṇaṃ. Saraṇagatānaṃ teneva saraṇagamanena bhayaṃ santāsaṃ dukkhaṃ duggatiparikilesaṃ hanati vināsetīti attho, ratanattayassevetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Atha vā hite pavattanena ahitā ca nivattanena sattānaṃ bhayaṃ hiṃsati buddho. Bhavakantārā uttāraṇena assāsadānena ca dhammo; appakānampi kārānaṃ vipulaphalapaṭilābhakaraṇena saṅgho . Tasmā imināpi pariyāyena ratanattayaṃ saraṇaṃ. Tappasādataggarutāhi vihatakileso tapparāyaṇatākārappavatto cittuppādo saraṇagamanaṃ. Taṃ samaṅgīsatto saraṇaṃ gacchati. Vuttappakārena cittuppādena etāni me tīṇi ratanāni saraṇaṃ, etāni parāyaṇanti evaṃ upetīti attho. Evaṃ tāva saraṇaṃ, saraṇagamanaṃ, yo ca saraṇaṃ gacchati, idaṃ tayaṃ veditabbaṃ. Saraṇagamanappabhede pana duvidhaṃ saraṇagamanaṃ – lokuttaraṃ lokiyañca. Tattha lokuttaraṃ diṭṭhasaccānaṃ maggakkhaṇe saraṇagamanupakkilesasamucchedena ārammaṇato nibbānārammaṇaṃ hutvā kiccato sakalepi ratanattaye ijjhati. Lokiyaṃ puthujjanānaṃ saraṇagamanupakkilesavikkhambhanena ārammaṇato buddhādiguṇārammaṇaṃ hutvā ijjhati. Taṃ atthato buddhādīsu vatthūsu saddhāpaṭilābho saddhāmūlikā ca sammādiṭṭhi dasasu puññakiriyavatthūsu diṭṭhijukammanti vuccati. Tayidaṃ catudhā vattati – attasanniyyātanena, tapparāyaṇatāya, sissabhāvūpagamanena, paṇipātenāti. Tattha attasanniyyātanaṃ nāma – ‘‘ajjādiṃ katvā ahaṃ attānaṃ buddhassa niyyātemi, dhammassa, saṅghassā’’ti evaṃ buddhādīnaṃ attapariccajanaṃ. Tapparāyaṇatā nāma ‘‘ajjādiṃ katvā ‘ahaṃ buddhaparāyaṇo, dhammaparāyaṇo, saṅghaparāyaṇo’ti. Maṃ dhārethā’’ti evaṃ tapparāyaṇabhāvo. Sissabhāvūpagamanaṃ nāma – ‘‘ajjādiṃ katvā – ‘ahaṃ buddhassa antevāsiko, dhammassa, saṅghassa antevāsiko’ti maṃ dhārethā’’ti evaṃ sissabhāvūpagamo. Paṇipāto nāma – ‘‘ajjādiṃ katvā ahaṃ abhivādanapaccuṭṭhānaañjalikammasāmīcikammaṃ buddhādīnaṃyeva tiṇṇaṃ vatthūnaṃ karomī’ti maṃ dhārethā’’ti evaṃ buddhādīsu paramanipaccākāro. Imesañhi catunnaṃ ākārānaṃ aññatarampi karontena gahitaṃyeva hoti saraṇaṃ. Api ca bhagavato attānaṃ pariccajāmi, dhammassa, saṅghassa, attānaṃ pariccajāmi, jīvitaṃ pariccajāmi, pariccattoyeva me attā, pariccattaṃyeva jīvitaṃ, jīvitapariyantikaṃ buddhaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmi, buddho me saraṇaṃ leṇaṃ tāṇanti ; evampi attasanniyyātanaṃ veditabbaṃ. ‘‘Satthārañca vatāhaṃ passeyyaṃ, bhagavantameva passeyyaṃ, sugatañca vatāhaṃ passeyyaṃ, bhagavantameva passeyyaṃ, sammāsambuddhañca vatāhaṃ passeyyaṃ, bhagavantameva passeyya’’nti (saṃ. ni. 2.154). Evampi mahākassapassa saraṇagamanaṃ viya sissabhāvūpagamanaṃ veditabbaṃ. Evampi āḷavakādīnaṃ saraṇagamanaṃ viya tapparāyaṇatā veditabbā. Atha kho brahmāyu brāhmaṇo uṭṭhāyāsanā ekaṃsaṃ uttarāsaṅgaṃ karitvā bhagavato pādesu sirasā nipatitvā bhagavato pādāni mukhena ca paricumbati, pāṇīhi ca parisambāhati, nāmañca sāveti – ‘‘brahmāyu ahaṃ, bho gotama brāhmaṇo, brahmāyu ahaṃ, bho gotama brāhmaṇo’’ti (ma. ni. 2.394) evampi paṇipāto daṭṭhabbo. So panesa ñātibhayācariyadakkhiṇeyyavasena catubbidho hoti. Tattha dakkhiṇeyyapaṇipātena saraṇagamanaṃ hoti, na itarehi. Seṭṭhavaseneva hi saraṇaṃ gaṇhāti, seṭṭhavasena ca bhijjati. Tasmā yo sākiyo vā koliyo vā – ‘‘buddho amhākaṃ ñātako’’ti vandati, aggahitameva hoti saraṇaṃ. Yo vā – ‘‘samaṇo gotamo rājapūjito mahānubhāvo avandīyamāno anatthampi kareyyā’’ti bhayena vandati, aggahitameva hoti saraṇaṃ. Yo vā bodhisattakāle bhagavato santike kiñci uggahitaṃ saramāno buddhakāle vā – Evarūpaṃ anusāsaniṃ uggahetvā – ‘‘ācariyo me’’ti vandati, aggahitameva hoti saraṇaṃ. Yo pana – ‘‘ayaṃ loke aggadakkhiṇeyyo’’ti vandati, teneva gahitaṃ hoti saraṇaṃ. Evaṃ gahitasaraṇassa ca upāsakassa vā upāsikāya vā aññatitthiyesu pabbajitampi ñātiṃ – ‘‘ñātako me aya’’nti vandato saraṇagamanaṃ na bhijjati, pageva apabbajitaṃ. Tathā rājānaṃ bhayavasena vandato. So hi raṭṭhapūjitattā avandīyamāno anatthampi kareyyāti. Tathā yaṃ kiñci sippaṃ sikkhāpakaṃ titthiyampi – ‘‘ācariyo me aya’’nti vandatopi na bhijjati, evaṃ saraṇagamanappabhedo veditabbo. Ettha ca lokuttarassa saraṇagamanassa cattāri sāmaññaphalāni vipākaphalaṃ, sabbadukkhakkhayo ānisaṃsaphalaṃ. Vuttañhetaṃ – Api ca niccādito anupagamanādivasena petassa ānisaṃsaphalaṃ veditabbaṃ. Vuttañhetaṃ – ‘‘aṭṭhānametaṃ anavakāso, yaṃ diṭṭhisampanno puggalo kañci saṅkhāraṃ niccato upagaccheyya…pe… kañci saṅkhāraṃ sukhato…pe… kañci dhammaṃ attato upagaccheyya…pe… mātaraṃ jīvitā voropeyya…pe… pitaraṃ…pe… arahantaṃ…pe… paduṭṭhacitto tathāgatassa lohitaṃ uppādeyya…pe…. saṅghaṃ bhindeyya…pe… aññaṃ satthāraṃ uddiseyya, netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjatī’’ti (a. ni. 1.290). Lokiyassa pana saraṇagamanassa bhavasampadāpi bhogasampadāpi phalameva. Vuttañhetaṃ – Aparampi vuttaṃ – ‘‘atha kho sakko devānamindo asītiyā devatāsahassehi saddhiṃ yenāyasmā mahāmoggallāno tenupasaṅkami…pe… ekamantaṃ ṭhitaṃ kho sakkaṃ devānamindaṃ āyasmā mahāmoggallāno etadavoca – ‘‘sādhu kho, devānaminda, buddhaṃ saraṇagamanaṃ hoti. Buddhaṃ saraṇagamanahetu kho, devānaminda, evamidhekacce sattā kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā sugatiṃ saggaṃ lokaṃ upapajjanti…pe… te aññe deve dasahi ṭhānehi adhigaṇhanti – dibbena āyunā, dibbena vaṇṇena, dibbena sukhena, dibbena yasena, dibbena ādhipateyyena, dibbehi rūpehi saddehi gandhehi rasehi phoṭṭhabbehī’’ti (saṃ. ni. 4.341). Esa nayo dhamme ca saṅghe ca. Api ca velāmasuttādīnaṃ vasenāpi saraṇagamanassa phalaviseso veditabbo. Evaṃ saraṇagamanassa phalaṃ veditabbaṃ. Tattha ca lokiyasaraṇagamanaṃ tīsu vatthūsu aññāṇasaṃsayamicchāñāṇādīhi saṃkilissati, na mahājutikaṃ hoti, na mahāvipphāraṃ. Lokuttarassa natthi saṃkileso. Lokiyassa ca saraṇagamanassa duvidho bhedo – sāvajjo ca anavajjo ca. Tattha sāvajjo aññasatthārādīsu attasanniyyātanādīhi hoti, so ca aniṭṭhaphalo hoti. Anavajjo kālakiriyāya hoti, so avipākattā aphalo. Lokuttarassa pana nevatthi bhedo. Bhavantarepi hi ariyasāvako aññaṃ satthāraṃ na uddisatīti. Evaṃ saraṇagamanassa saṃkileso ca bhedo ca veditabboti. Upāsakaṃ maṃ bhante bhagavā dhāretūti maṃ bhagavā ‘‘upāsako aya’’nti evaṃ dhāretu, jānātūti attho. Upāsakavidhikosallatthaṃ panettha – ko upāsako? Kasmā upāsakoti vuccati ? Kimassa sīlaṃ? Ko ājīvo? Kā vipatti? Kā sampattīti? Idaṃ pakiṇṇakaṃ veditabbaṃ. Tattha ko upāsakoti yo koci saraṇagato gahaṭṭho. Vuttañhetaṃ – ‘‘yato kho, mahānāma, buddhaṃ saraṇaṃ gato hoti, dhammaṃ saraṇaṃ gato hoti, saṅghaṃ saraṇaṃ gato hoti. Ettāvatā kho, mahānāma, upāsako hotī’’ti (saṃ. ni. 5.1033). Kasmā upāsakoti ratanattayaṃ upāsanato. So hi buddhaṃ upāsatīti upāsako, tathā dhammaṃ saṃghaṃ. Kimassasīlanti pañca veramaṇiyo. Yathāha – ‘‘yato kho, mahānāma, upāsako pāṇātipātā paṭivirato hoti, adinnādānā… kāmesumicchācārā… musāvādā… surāmerayamajjapamādaṭṭhānā paṭivirato hoti, ettāvatā kho, mahānāma, upāsako sīlavā hotī’’ti (saṃ. ni. 5.1033). Koājīvoti pañca micchāvaṇijjā pahāya dhammena samena jīvitakappanaṃ. Vuttañhetaṃ – ‘‘pañcimā, bhikkhave, vaṇijjā upāsakena akaraṇīyā. Katamā pañca? Satthavaṇijjā, sattavaṇijjā, maṃsavaṇijjā, majjavaṇijjā, visavaṇijjā. Imā kho, bhikkhave, pañca vaṇijjā upāsakena akaraṇīyā’’ti (a. ni. 5.177). Kā vipattīti yā tasseva sīlassa ca ājīvassa ca vipatti, ayamassa vipatti. Api ca yāya esa caṇḍālo ceva hoti, malañca patikuṭṭho ca, sāpissa vipattīti veditabbā. Te ca atthato assaddhiyādayo pañca dhammā honti. Yathāha – ‘‘pañcahi, bhikkhave, dhammehi samannāgato upāsako upāsakacaṇḍālo ca hoti, upāsakamalañca, upāsakapatikuṭṭho ca. Katamehi pañcahi? Assaddho hoti, dussīlo hoti, kotūhalamaṅgaliko hoti, maṅgalaṃ pacceti, no kammaṃ, ito ca bahiddhā dakkhiṇeyyaṃ pariyesati, tattha ca pubbakāraṃ karotī’’ti (a. ni. 5.175). Kā sampattīti yā cassa sīlasampadā ceva ājīvasampadā ca, sā sampatti; ye cassa ratanabhāvādikarā saddhādayo pañca dhammā. Yathāha – ‘‘pañcahi, bhikkhave, dhammehi samannāgato upāsako upāsakaratanañca hoti, upāsakapadumañca, upāsakapuṇḍarīkañca. Katamehi pañcahi? Saddho hoti, sīlavā hoti, na kotūhalamaṅgaliko hoti, kammaṃ pacceti, no maṅgalaṃ, na ito bahiddhā dakkhiṇeyyaṃ gavesati, idha ca pubbakāraṃ karotī’’ti (a. ni. 5.175). Ajjataggeti etthāyaṃ aggasaddo ādikoṭikoṭṭhāsaseṭṭhesu dissati. ‘‘Ajjatagge, samma dovārika, āvarāmi dvāraṃ nigaṇṭhānaṃ nigaṇṭhīna’’ntiādīsu (ma. ni. 2.70) hi ādimhi dissati. ‘‘Teneva aṅgulaggena taṃ aṅgulaggaṃ parāmaseyya . Ucchaggaṃ veḷagga’’ntiādīsu (kathā. 281) koṭiyaṃ. ‘‘Ambilaggaṃ vā madhuraggaṃ vā tittakaggaṃ vā vihāraggena vā pariveṇaggena vā bhājetu’’ntiādīsu (cūḷava. 317) koṭṭhāse. ‘‘Yāvatā, bhikkhave, sattā apadā vā…pe… tathāgato tesaṃ aggamakkhāyatī’’tiādīsu (a. ni. 4.34) seṭṭhe. Idha panāyaṃ ādimhi daṭṭhabbo. Tasmā ajjataggeti ajjataṃ ādiṃ katvāti evametthattho veditabbo. Ajjatanti ajjabhāvaṃ. Ajjadaggeti vā pāṭho, dakāro padasandhikaro. Ajja agganti attho. Pāṇupetanti pāṇehi upetaṃ. Yāva me jīvitaṃ pavattati, tāva upetaṃ anaññasatthukaṃ tīhi saraṇagamanehi saraṇaṃ gataṃ upāsakaṃ kappiyakārakaṃ maṃ bhagavā dhāretu jānātu. Ahañhi sacepi me tikhiṇena asinā sīsaṃ chindeyya, neva buddhaṃ ‘‘na buddho’’ti vā, dhammaṃ ‘‘na dhammo’’ti vā, saṅghaṃ ‘‘na saṅgho’’ti vā vadeyyanti. Evaṃ attasanniyyātanena saraṇaṃ gantvā attanā kataṃ aparādhaṃ pakāsento accayo maṃ, bhantetiādimāha. Tattha accayoti aparādho. Maṃ accagamāti maṃ atikkamma abhibhavitvā pavatto. Dhammikaṃ dhammarājānanti ettha dhammaṃ caratīti dhammiko. Dhammeneva rājā jāto, na pitughātanādinā adhammenāti dhammarājā. Jīvitā voropesinti jīvitā viyojesiṃ. Paṭiggaṇhātūti khamatu. Āyatiṃ saṃvarāyāti anāgate saṃvaratthāya. Puna evarūpassa aparādhassa dosassa khalitassa akaraṇatthāya.

The king, applauding here and there, having carefully listened to the beginning, middle, and end, thought: “For a long time, while asking various ascetics and Brahmins these questions, I did not find any essence, as if threshing chaff. Oh, the Blessed One is endowed with a wealth of virtues! He has answered these questions of mine creating a great light, as if lighting a thousand lamps for me."

"For a long time, without knowing the power of the ten strengths of the Buddha, I have been deceived!” Thinking thus, his body was filled with five kinds of rapture born of recollecting the Buddha’s virtues, and revealing his own confidence, he declared himself a lay follower ( upāsaka).

To show this, the passage that begins “When the Exalted One had finished speaking” is undertaken.

There, abhikkantaṃ, bhante—this word abhikkanta is seen in the senses of exhaustion, excellence, handsomeness, and approval.

"Excellent, venerable sir, is the night; the first watch has ended; the Community of bhikkhus has been sitting long" and so on (A.
Ni.

20) it is seen in the sense of exhaustion.

“This person is pleasing to me, and is more excellent and refined than these four persons” and so on (A.
Ni.
4.
100) in the sense of excellence.

In the beginning, it is handsome.

"Excellent, Venerable Gotama," and so on (Pārā.
15) in the sense of approval.

Here too, it is indeed in the sense of approval.

Since it is in the sense of approval, therefore, it should be understood that “Sādhu, sādhu, bhante” has been said.

By means of this characteristic, here, by way of confidence and by way of praise, this is said twice; thus it should be understood.

Or else, abhikkantaṃ means abhikantaṃ, very lovely, very desirable, very pleasing, very excellent; thus it is said.

Here, with one exclamation of abhikkanta, he praises the teaching, and with the other, his own confidence.

And here is the meaning: "Excellent, venerable sir, is the Blessed One's teaching of the Dhamma; 'excellent' is my confidence, having come to the Blessed One's teaching of the Dhamma."

Or else, the word of the Blessed One itself, referring in each case to a double meaning.

The Blessed One’s word is excellent because it destroys faults, excellent because it leads to the acquisition of virtues.

Similarly, because it generates faith, generates wisdom, is meaningful, is well-phrased, has clear terms, has deep meaning, is pleasing to the ear, wins the heart, does not extol oneself, does not disparage others, is cooled by compassion, is cleansed by wisdom, is delightful to hear, can withstand examination, is pleasant when heard, and is beneficial when investigated—thus it should be connected, and so on.

Then, further on, he praises the teaching itself with four similes.

There, nikkujjitaṃ means placed with the face downwards, or with the face born underneath.

Ukkujjeyya means one should make the face upwards.

Paṭicchannaṃ means covered with grass, leaves, and so on.

Vivareyya means would uncover.

Mūḷhassa vā means to one who is confused or lost in the directions.

Maggaṃ ācikkheyya means having taken him by the hand, he would say, "This is the path." In darkness means in a fourfold darkness, on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, in the middle of the night, with thickets of forests, masses of clouds.

This, first of all, is the meaning without elaboration.

But this is the interpretation with purport.

Just as someone would turn upright what is upside down, so too, he raised me, who had turned away from the good Dhamma and had fallen into the bad Dhamma, from the bad Dhamma.

Just as he would reveal what is covered, so too, by revealing the sāsana that had been covered by the thicket of wrong views since the disappearance of the sāsana of the Blessed Kassapa, just as he would point out the path to one who is confused, so too, by revealing to me, who had embarked on the wrong path, the false path, the path to heaven and liberation, just as he would hold an oil lamp in the darkness, so too, by holding the lamp of the teaching that dispels the darkness of delusion, for me who was immersed in the darkness of delusion and did not see the forms of the Buddha and other jewels, the Blessed One has revealed the Dhamma in many ways because of being manifested by these methods.

Having thus praised the teaching, being with pleased mind with this teaching in the three jewels, doing a pleased way, he spoke esāhantiādi.

There, esāhanti means this I.

“I go to the Blessed One for refuge” means the Blessed One is my refuge, my supreme resort, the destroyer of misery, and the provider of welfare.

With this intention, I go to the Blessed One, I worship, I serve, I attend upon him; or else, thus I know, I understand.
Because for those linguistic roots which have the meaning of ‘ travelling ’ have also the meaning of ‘ discovering ’.
Therefore it is said that “I go” can also mean “I know, I understand.”
The word “Dhamma” is derived from the verb “supports” , because it supports those who have achieved the path, who have realized cessation, who are practicing as instructed, preventing them from falling into the four planes of misery. In denotation, the Dhamma is the noble path and Nibbāna.
For this has been said: “Bhikkhus, to whatever extent there are things which are conditioned, the Noble Eightfold Path is declared the best of them” in detail.
The Dhamma is not only the noble path and Nibbāna,
but also the scriptural Dhamma together with the noble fruits.
For this is said in the Chattamāṇavaka Vimāna: Here, “the fading of lust” is the path.
“The wishless and the sorrowless” is the fruit.
“The unconditioned state” is Nibbāna.
And the “attractive, sweet, potent, well analyzed” is the aggregates of Dhamma analyzed into the three Piṭakas.
The Saṅgha consists of those who are united through unity of view and moral discipline. In denotation, it is the assembly of the eight noble individuals.
For this is said in that same Vimāna: the Saṅgha of bhikkhus is the bhikkhusaṅgha.
To this extent the king has declared his threefold going for refuge.
In order to gain proficiency with regard to going for refuge, the following method of exposition should be understood: the refuge, the going for refuge, the one who goes for refuge, the analysis of going for refuge, the fruit of going for refuge, the defilement, and the breach. This is the method to be understood.
As to the refuge: it slays, thus it is a refuge.
The meaning is that for those who have gone for refuge it kills and destroys their fear, terror, and suffering, and the affliction of a bad destination. “Refuge” is a designation for the Triple Gem ( ratana-ttaya).
Or alternatively, the Buddha slays the fear of beings by promoting their welfare and by preventing their harm.
The Dhamma does so by enabling them to cross the desert of existence and by giving them comfort, and the Saṃgha by making even small religious acts yield the gain of abundant fruit.
Therefore, in this way too, the Triple Gem ( ratana-ttaya) is a refuge.
The going for refuge is an act of consciousness which, through confidence in and reverence for the Triple Gem ( ratana-ttaya), is devoid of defilements and occurs in the mode of regarding the Triple Gem ( ratana-ttaya) as the supreme resort.
The one who goes for refuge is a being endowed with that.
The meaning is one who approaches with the aforesaid act of consciousness thus: “This Triple Gem ( ratana-ttaya) is my refuge, this is my supreme resort.”
Thus, first of all, the refuge, the going for refuge, and he who goes for refuge: this triad is to be understood.
In the analysis of the going for refuge, the going for refuge is twofold, the supramundane ( lokuttaraṃ) and the mundane ( lokiyañca).
The supramundane going for refuge is achieved at the moment of the path by those who have seen the truths, through the eradication of the defilements of the going for refuge; by way of its object, it takes Nibbāna as its objects, and by way of its task, it succeeds in regard to the entire Triple Gem ( ratana-ttaya).
The mundane going for refuge is achieved by worldlings through the suppression of the defilements of the going for refuge; by way of its object, it takes as its object the excellent qualities of the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṃgha.
In denotation, it is the gaining of faith in the objects of faith—the Buddha, etc.—and right view rooted in faith, referred to as the “straightening of view” among the ten bases of meritorious activity.
This mundane going for refuge occurs in four ways: by self-surrender, by taking the Triple Gem ( ratana-ttaya) as one’s supreme resort, by the acceptance of pupilship, and by homage by prostration.
Therein, self-surrender is the relinquishing of oneself to the Triple Gem ( ratana-ttaya), expressed thus: “From today onward I surrender myself to the Buddha, to the Dhamma, and to the Saṃgha.” Thus is the relinquishing of self to the Buddha etc.
Taking the Triple Gem ( ratana-ttaya) as one’s supreme resort is expressed thus: “From today onward the Buddha is my supreme resort, the Dhamma is my supreme resort, the Saṃgha is my supreme resort.
Thus may you know me!" Thus is the state of taking the Triple Gem ( ratana-ttaya) as one’s supreme resort.
” The acceptance of pupilship is expressed thus: “From today onward I am a pupil of the Buddha, a pupil of the Dhamma, a pupil of the Saṃgha. Thus may you know me!
” Homage by prostration is the quality of deepest humility towards the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṃgha, expressed thus: “From today onward I do homage, rise up in respect, show reverential salutation, and perform the proper duties only towards the three objects of refuge: the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṃgha. Thus may you know me!
” Refuge is taken by acting in any of these four ways.
Further, self-surrender may be understood through such expressions as the following: “I relinquish myself to the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṃgha. I relinquish my life to them. My self has been relinquished to them, my life has been relinquished to them. Until the end of my life, I go for refuge to the Buddha. The Buddha is my refuge, my shelter, my protection.”
“I would see the Teacher, the Exalted One! I would see the Accomplished One, the Exalted One! I would see the Perfectly Enlightened One, the Exalted One! ”.2.154)
Thus, acceptance of pupilship may be understood through the example of Mahākassapa’s going for refuge.
Taking the Triple Gem as one’s supreme resort may be understood through the example of the going for refuge of Āḷavaka, etc.
Then the brahmin Brahmāyu rose from his seat, and after arranging his upper robe on one shoulder, he prostrated himself with his head at the Blessed One’s feet, and he covered the Blessed One’s feet with kisses and caressed them with his hands, pronouncing his name: “I am the brahmin Brahmāyu, Master Gotama; I am the brahmin Brahmāyu, Master Gotama.” (Ma.
Ni.
2.394) Homage by prostration may be illustrated thus.
Homage by prostration may be of four kinds: that shown towards a relative, that motivated by fear, that shown towards a teacher, and that based on esteem for spiritual worthiness.
Of these, homage by prostration based on esteem for spiritual worthiness constitutes the going for refuge, not the others.
For one takes refuge only by way of the highest and breaks it only by way of the highest.
Therefore, if a member of the Sākya or Koliya clan venerates the Buddha thinking, “He is our relative,” he has not thereby taken refuge.
Or if one venerates the Buddha out of fear, thinking, “The recluse Gotama is worshipped by kings and has great power; if I do not venerate him, he may harm me,” one has not taken refuge.
Or if in the time of the Bodhisattva he, remembering something he had learned in the Blessed One’s presence, or in the Buddha-time, having learned a teaching of this kind, venerates (him), (thinking): “He is my teacher,” even then refuge is not taken.
But if one pays worship to the Buddha in the conviction “This is the most venerable being in the world,” only by such a one is refuge taken.
A male or female lay devotee who has taken refuge in the Triple Gem, worships a relative, thinking: “He is my kinsman.” Even if that relative is a recluse of another faith, the refuge in the Triple Gem is unbroken; still less can it be said to be broken if it is not a recluse or a priest.
So, too, the refuge is not broken if one venerates a king out of fear.
When prostrating before a king, out of fear: “If he who is honored by the whole country is not worshipped, he will do me harm!” — in that case too the refuge is unbroken.
Nor if one venerates a sectarian teacher from whom one has learned a craft, thinking, “He is my teacher.” Thus the analysis of the going for refuge should be understood.
The fruit of going for refuge should be understood as follows. In the case of the supramundane going for refuge that is, the noble path, the four fruits of recluseship are the resultant-fruit, 82 the destruction of all suffering is the benefit-fruit.
Further, the benefit-fruit of the going for refuge may be understood by way of “not approaching any formations as permanent,” etc.
For this is said: “It is impossible, it cannot come to pass, that an individual who has attained to right view might approach any formation as permanent, any formation as pleasurable, any phenomenon as self. It is impossible, it cannot come to pass, that he might deprive his mother of life, that he might deprive his father of life, that he might deprive an arahat of life, that with a mind of hatred he might shed a Tathāgata’s blood, that he might create a schism in the Saṃgha, that he might point out another teacher. There is no possibility of that” (A.
Ni.
1.290).
But the fruit of the mundane refuge is only the attainment of favorable rebirth, and the attainment of property and enjoyment.
It is also said: “Then Sakka, the king of the gods, together with eighty-thousand deities approached venerable Mahāmoggallāna … who told him: ‘It is good, O lord of the gods, to go for refuge to the Buddha.
Because of going for refuge to the Buddha, some beings here, with the breakup of the body, reappear after death in a good destination, in a heavenly world. They surpass the other gods in ten respects: in divine life span, in divine beauty, in divine pleasure, in divine fame, in divine sovereignty, and in divine forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and tangibles’” (Saṃ.
Ni.
4.341).
The same method applies in going for refuge to the Dhamma and the Saṃgha.
Further, the distinctive fruit of going for refuge should be understood by way of the Velāma Sutta, etc. where the Buddha says that going for refuge is more fruitful than the most lavish acts of generosity.
Thus the fruit of going for refuge should be understood.
In regard to defilement, the mundane going for refuge is defiled by ignorance, doubt, misunderstanding, etc., concerning the three objects of faith; thus it does not become very luminous and pervasive.
The supramundane refuge is free from any defilements.
The breach of the mundane going for refuge is of two kinds, blameworthy and blameless.
The blameworthy comes about when one surrenders oneself, etc., to another teacher, etc.; this has undesirable fruits.
The blameless occurs when one dies; because this does not produce kammic results it is without fruit.
But there is no breach of the supramundane going for refuge.
Even in another existence a noble disciple will not turn to another teacher.
Thus, the defilement and the breach of the going for refuge should be understood.
“Let the Exalted One accept me as a lay follower (upāsakaṃ)”, the meaning is: “Let the Exalted One accept me thus, ‘He is a lay follower’; let him know me thus.”
Here, for the purpose of skill in the procedure of a lay follower: What is a lay follower (upāsaka)? Why is he called a lay follower (upāsaka)? What is his moral discipline (śīla)? What is his livelihood (ājīva)? What is his failure (vipatti)? What is his success (sampatti)? This miscellaneous matter should be understood.
There, who is a lay follower (upāsaka)? Any householder who has gone for refuge (saraṇagato).
Thus it is said: “Mahānāma, when one has gone for refuge (saraṇaṃ gato) to the Buddha, gone for refuge (saraṇaṃ gato) to the Dhamma, and gone for refuge (saraṇaṃ gato) to the Saṃgha,
to this extent one is a lay follower (upāsako hoti)” (Saṃ.
Ni.
5.
1033).
Why is he called “lay follower (upāsaka)”? Because he has drawn near to the Triple Gem (ratanattayaṃ upāsanato).
For he draws near to the Buddha, thus he is a lay follower (upāsako), and likewise to the Dhamma and the Saṃgha.
What is his moral discipline (śīla)? The five abstinences (pañca veramaṇiyo).
As it is said: “Mahānāma, when a lay follower (upāsako) abstains from the destruction of life (pāṇātipātā paṭivirato hoti), from taking what is not given (adinnādānā…), from sexual misconduct (kāmesumicchācārā…), from false speech (musāvādā…), and from fermented and distilled intoxicants which are the basis for heedlessness (surāmerayamajjapamādaṭṭhānā paṭivirato hoti), to this extent a lay follower (upāsako sīlavā hoti) is morally disciplined” (Saṃ.
Ni.
5.
1033).
What is his livelihood (ājīvo)? Having abandoned five kinds of wrong trade (pañca micchāvaṇijjā pahāya), he earns his living righteously, in accordance with the Dhamma (dhammena samena jīvitakappanaṃ).
Thus it is said: “Bhikkhus, these five trades (pañcimā, bhikkhave, vaṇijjā) should not be engaged in by a lay follower (upāsakena akaraṇīyā).
Which are the five (katamā pañca)? Trading in weapons (satthavaṇijjā), trading in beings (sattavaṇijjā), trading in meat (maṃsavaṇijjā), trading in intoxicants (majjavaṇijjā), and trading in poisons (visavaṇijjā).
These are the five trades (imā kho, bhikkhave, pañca vaṇijjā) which should not be engaged in by a lay follower (upāsakena akaraṇīyā)” (A.
Ni.
5.
177).
What is his failure (vipatti)? Failure in his moral discipline (sīlassa ca) and in his livelihood (ājīvassa ca vipatti), this is his failure (vipatti).
Further, that which makes him an outcast (caṇḍālo), stained (malañca) and repulsive (patikuṭṭho ca), that too is his failure (vipattīti veditabbā).
This refers to the five qualities (pañca dhammā), such as lack of faith (assaddhiyādayo), etc.
As it is said: “Bhikkhus, possessed of five qualities (pañcahi, bhikkhave, dhammehi samannāgato), a lay follower (upāsako) is an outcast lay follower (upāsakacaṇḍālo ca hoti), a stained lay follower (upāsakamalañca), a repulsive lay follower (upāsakapatikuṭṭho ca).
Which are the five (katamehi pañcahi)? He lacks faith (assaddho hoti); he is immoral (dussīlo hoti); he believes in superstitious omens (kotūhalamaṅgaliko hoti); he relies on omens (maṅgalaṃ pacceti), not on kamma (no kammaṃ); he seeks spiritually worthy persons (dakkhiṇeyyaṃ pariyesati) outside of here, and he shows honor there first (tattha ca pubbakāraṃ karotī)” (A.
Ni.
5.
175).
What is his success (sampattīti)? Success in his moral discipline (sīlasampadā ceva) and success in his livelihood (ājīvasampadā ca), this is his success (sā sampatti); so too are the five qualities (pañca dhammā), such as faith (saddhādayo), etc., which make him a gem (ratanabhāvādikarā), etc.
As it is said: “Bhikkhus, possessed of five qualities (pañcahi, bhikkhave, dhammehi samannāgato), a lay follower (upāsako) is a gem-like lay follower (upāsakaratanañca hoti), a red lotus-like lay follower (upāsakapadumañca), and a white lotus-like lay follower (upāsakapuṇḍarīkañca).
Which are the five (katamehi pañcahi)? He has faith (saddho hoti); he is morally disciplined (sīlavā hoti); he does not believe in superstitious omens (na kotūhalamaṅgaliko hoti); he relies on kamma (kammaṃ pacceti), not on omens (no maṅgalaṃ); he does not seek spiritually worthy persons (dakkhiṇeyyaṃ gavesati) outside of here, and he shows honor here first (idha ca pubbakāraṃ karotī)” (A.
Ni.

175).

Today [is] the foremost, [this is the] meaning.
Pāṇupetaṃ means endowed with life.
As long as my life continues, may the Blessed One accept me and know me as a lay follower ( upāsaka) who has approached [the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha] and gone for refuge by means of the three refuges, who has no other teacher, who is a fitting attendant.
If even someone were to cut off my head with a sharp sword, even then I would not say that the Buddha is "not the Buddha," or the dharma is "not the dharma," or the saṃgha is "not the saṃgha."
Thus, having gone for refuge by self-surrender, revealing the offense done by himself, the king spoke, saying, "The transgression is mine, O Blessed One," and so on.
There, accayo means offense ( aparādha).
"The transgression has overtaken me" means having transgressed me, having overcome [me], it has arisen.
Dhammikaṃ dhammarājānaṃ, here dhammika means one who practices the dharma.
The king was born by means of dharma indeed, not by adharma, such as killing his father, therefore [he is a] righteous king ( dharmarāja).
They deprived [him] of life, they separated [him] from life.
"May he accept," [means] may he forgive.
Āyatiṃ saṃvarāya means for restraint in the future.
Again, for the sake of not doing such an offense, fault, slip.
251
251. ‘‘Taggha tvaṃ, mahārāja, accayo accagamā yathābālaṃ yathāmūḷhaṃ yathāakusalaṃ, yaṃ tvaṃ pitaraṃ dhammikaṃ dhammarājānaṃ jīvitā voropesi. Yato ca kho tvaṃ, mahārāja, accayaṃ accayato disvā yathādhammaṃ paṭikarosi, taṃ te mayaṃ paṭiggaṇhāma. Vuddhihesā, mahārāja, ariyassa vinaye, yo accayaṃ accayato disvā yathādhammaṃ paṭikaroti, āyatiṃ saṃvaraṃ āpajjatī’’ti.
“Indeed, great king, a transgression ( accaya) overcame you. You acted as a fool (yathābālaṃ), as one deluded (yathāmūḷhaṃ), as one unskilled (yathāakusalaṃ), because you deprived your father, a righteous man (dhammikaṃ) and a righteous king (dhammarājānaṃ), of his life (jīvitā).

But since you, great king, have recognized your transgression (accayaṃ) as a transgression (accayato) and make amends (paṭikarosi) according to the Dharma (yathādhammaṃ), we accept (paṭiggaṇhāma) it from you.

For, great king, this is growth (vuddhihesā) in the discipline (vinaye) of the Noble One (ariyassa): that one sees one’s transgression (accayaṃ) as a transgression (accayato), makes amends (paṭikaroti) according to the Dharma (yathādhammaṃ), and undertakes (āpajjati) restraint (saṃvaraṃ) for the future (āyatiṃ.”
251.Tagghāti ekaṃse nipāto. Yathā dhammaṃ paṭikarosīti yathā dhammo ṭhito tatheva karosi, khamāpesīti vuttaṃ hoti. Taṃ te mayaṃ paṭiggaṇhāmāti taṃ tava aparādhaṃ mayaṃ khamāma. Vuḍḍhihesā, mahārāja ariyassa vinayeti esā, mahārāja, ariyassa vinaye buddhassa bhagavato sāsane vuḍḍhi nāma. Katamā? Yāyaṃ accayaṃ accayato disvā yathādhammaṃ paṭikaritvā āyatiṃ saṃvarāpajjanā, desanaṃ pana puggalādhiṭṭhānaṃ karonto – ‘‘yo accayaṃ accayato disvā yathādhammaṃ paṭikaroti, āyatiṃ saṃvaraṃ āpajjatī’’ti āha.
251.
Indeed, this is a particle indicating certainty.

"As you make amends according to the Dhamma" means you act as the Dhamma dictates, you ask for forgiveness.

"We accept that from you" means we forgive that offense of yours.

“This, great king, is called growth in the discipline of the Noble One (ariyassa vinaye), in the dispensation (sāsane) of the Exalted Buddha (buddhassa bhagavato).”

Which one? It is when, having seen a transgression (accayaṃ) as a transgression (accayato), one makes amends according to the Dhamma (yathādhammaṃ), and undertakes restraint (saṃvara) in the future (āyatiṃ); moreover, when giving instruction (desanaṃ) based on the individual (puggalādhiṭṭhānaṃ), one says: "Whoever, having seen a transgression (accayaṃ) as a transgression (accayato), makes amends according to the Dhamma (yathādhammaṃ), undertakes restraint (saṃvaraṃ) in the future (āyatiṃ)."
252
252. Evaṃ vutte, rājā māgadho ajātasattu vedehiputto bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – ‘‘handa ca dāni mayaṃ, bhante, gacchāma bahukiccā mayaṃ bahukaraṇīyā’’ti. ‘‘Yassadāni tvaṃ, mahārāja, kālaṃ maññasī’’ti. Atha kho rājā māgadho ajātasattu vedehiputto bhagavato bhāsitaṃ abhinanditvā anumoditvā uṭṭhāyāsanā bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā padakkhiṇaṃ katvā pakkāmi.
When this was said, King Ajātaśatru (Ajātasattu), son of Vaidehī, the king of Magadha, said to the Blessed One (bhagavantaṃ): “Now, venerable sir (bhante), we must go. We have many tasks and duties.”

“Now is the time, great king (mahārāja), to do as you think fit.” (‘‘yassadāni tvaṃ, mahārāja, kālaṃ maññasī’’ti.)

Then King Ajātaśatru (Ajātasattu), son of Vaidehī, the king of Magadha, having delighted and rejoiced in the word of the Blessed One (bhagavato bhāsitaṃ), rose from his seat, and after paying homage to the Blessed One (bhagavantaṃ), circumambulated him, and departed.
252.Evaṃ vutteti evaṃ bhagavatā vutte. Handa ca dāni mayaṃ bhanteti ettha handāti vacasāyatthe nipāto. So hi gamanavacasāyaṃ katvā evamāha. Bahukiccāti balavakiccā. Bahukaraṇīyāti tasseva vevacanaṃ. Yassadāni tvanti yassa idāni tvaṃ mahārāja gamanassa kālaṃ maññasi jānāsi, tassa kālaṃ tvameva jānāsīti vuttaṃ hoti. Padakkhiṇaṃ katvā pakkāmīti tikkhattuṃ padakkhiṇaṃ katvā dasanakhasamodhānasamujjalaṃ añjaliṃ sirasi patiṭṭhapetvā yāva dassanavisayaṃ bhagavato abhimukhova paṭikkamitvā dassanavijahanaṭṭhānabhūmiyaṃ pañcapatiṭṭhitena vanditvā pakkāmi.
252.
Evaṃ vutte ti means: Thus, when it was spoken by the Blessed One.
Handa ca dāni mayaṃ bhante ti means: Here, handa is a particle implying acceptance of the word.
So hi gamanavacasāyaṃ katvā evamāha means: Having made the intention to leave, he spoke thus.
Bahukicca ti means: Having many duties, meaning weighty duties.
Bahukaraṇīya ti means: A synonym for that very thing.
Yassadāni tvanti means: "Now, Your Majesty, when do you think is the time for departure?" Meaning, "You alone know the time for that."
Padakkhiṇaṃ katvā pakkāmīti: Having circumambulated, he departed. That is, having circumambulated three times, and having placed his radiant joined palms (añjali) , where the ten fingernails were united, upon his head, and having retreated facing the Blessed One as far as the range of sight, and having paid homage with all five limbs on the ground at the place where he passed out of sight, he departed.
253
253. Atha kho bhagavā acirapakkantassa rañño māgadhassa ajātasattussa vedehiputtassa bhikkhū āmantesi – ‘‘khatāyaṃ, bhikkhave, rājā. Upahatāyaṃ, bhikkhave, rājā. Sacāyaṃ, bhikkhave, rājā pitaraṃ dhammikaṃ dhammarājānaṃ jīvitā na voropessatha, imasmiññeva āsane virajaṃ vītamalaṃ dhammacakkhuṃ uppajjissathā’’ti. Idamavoca bhagavā. Attamanā te bhikkhū bhagavato bhāsitaṃ abhinandunti.
253. Then, shortly after King Ajātaśatru, the son of Vaidehī, of Magadha, had departed, the Blessed One addressed the monks: "This king is ruined, monks.

He has injured himself, monks.

If this king had not deprived his father, a righteous (dhāmmika) and just king (dharmarājā), of his life, then in this very seat the dust-free, stainless Eye of Dharma (dharmacakṣu) would have arisen in him."

This is what the Blessed One said.

The monks, delighted, rejoiced at the Blessed One’s words.
253.Khatāyaṃ, bhikkhave, rājāti khato ayaṃ, bhikkhave, rājā. Upahatāyanti upahato ayaṃ. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – ayaṃ, bhikkhave, rājā khato upahato bhinnapatiṭṭho jāto, tathānena attanāva attā khato, yathā attano patiṭṭhā na jātāti. Virajanti rāgarajādivirahitaṃ. Rāgamalādīnaṃyeva vigatattā vītamalaṃ. Dhammacakkhunti dhammesu vā cakkhuṃ, dhammamayaṃ vā cakkhuṃ, aññesu ṭhānesu tiṇṇaṃ maggānametaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Idha pana sotāpattimaggasseva. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – sace iminā pitā ghātito nābhavissa, idāni idhevāsane nisinno sotāpattimaggaṃ patto abhavissa, pāpamittasaṃsaggena panassa antarāyo jāto. Evaṃ santepi yasmā ayaṃ tathāgataṃ upasaṅkamitvā ratanattayaṃ saraṇaṃ gato, tasmā mama sāsanamahantatāya yathā nāma koci purisassa vadhaṃ katvā pupphamuṭṭhimattena daṇḍena mucceyya, evameva lohakumbhiyaṃ nibbattitvā tiṃsavassasahassāni adho patanto heṭṭhimatalaṃ patvā tiṃsavassasahassāni uddhaṃ gacchanto punapi uparimatalaṃ pāpuṇitvā muccissatīti idampi kira bhagavatā vuttameva, pāḷiyaṃ pana na ārūḷhaṃ. Idaṃ pana suttaṃ sutvā raññā koci ānisaṃso laddhoti? Mahāānisaṃso laddho. Ayañhi pitu māritakālato paṭṭhāya neva rattiṃ na divā niddaṃ labhati, satthāraṃ pana upasaṅkamitvā imāya madhurāya ojavantiyā dhammadesanāya sutakālato paṭṭhāya niddaṃ labhi. Tiṇṇaṃ ratanānaṃ mahāsakkāraṃ akāsi. Pothujjanikāya saddhāya samannāgato nāma iminā raññā sadiso nāhosi. Anāgate pana vijitāvī nāma paccekabuddho hutvā parinibbāyissatīti . Idamavoca bhagavā. Attamanā te bhikkhū bhagavato bhāsitaṃ abhinandunti.
253.

“This king, monks, is ruined,” means this king, monks, is ruined.

“He has injured himself” means he has injured himself.

This is meant: “This king, monks, is ruined, injured, and has destroyed his support. Thus, he has ruined himself by himself alone, in such a way that he has no support.”

"Stainless" (virajanti) means devoid of stains such as lust (rāgarajādivirahitaṃ).

"Stainless" (vītamalaṃ) means being without stains, due to the absence of the stain of lust, and so on (rāgamalādīnaṃyeva vigatattā).

"Eye of the Dhamma" (dhammacakkhu) means the eye in phenomena (dhammesu), or the eye made by the Dhamma (dhammamayaṃ). In other places, this is a designation for the three lower paths (tiṇṇaṃ maggānaṃ etaṃ adhivacanaṃ).

Here, however, it is only for the path of stream-entry (sotāpattimaggassa).

This is meant: "If his father had not been murdered by him (iminā pitā ghātito), he would now, while sitting here in this very seat (idhevāsane nisinno), have attained the path of stream-entry (sotāpattimaggaṃ patto abhavissa). But because of associating with evil friends (pāpamittasaṃsaggena), an obstacle (antarāyo) has arisen for him."

Even so, because he approached the Thus Gone One (tathāgataṃ upasaṅkamitvā) and went for refuge to the Triple Gem (ratanattayaṃ saraṇaṃ gato), therefore, through the greatness of my dispensation (mama sāsanamahantatāya), just as someone who has committed murder (vadhaṃ katvā) might be freed by paying a fine consisting of a handful of flowers (pupphamuṭṭhimattena daṇḍena mucceyya), even so, having been born in the Hell of Copper Cauldrons (lohakumbhiyaṃ nibbattitvā), after falling downwards for thirty thousand years (tiṃsavassasahassāni adho patanto), having reached the bottom (heṭṭhimatalaṃ patvā), and ascending upwards for thirty thousand years (tiṃsavassasahassāni uddhaṃ gacchanto), having again reached the top (uparimatalaṃ pāpuṇitvā), he will be freed (muccissatīti)." This too, it is said, was spoken by the Blessed One (bhagavatā vuttameva), but it is not included in the Pāḷi (pāḷiyaṃ pana na ārūḷhaṃ).

Having heard this sutta (idaṃ pana suttaṃ sutvā), did the king gain any benefit (raññā koci ānisaṃso laddhoti)? He gained great benefit (mahāānisaṃso laddho).

For, from the time he killed his father (pitu māritakālato paṭṭhāya), he did not get any sleep (niddaṃ labhati), either by night (rattiṃ) or by day (divā). But from the time he approached the Teacher (satthāraṃ pana upasaṅkamitvā) and [heard] this sweet and nourishing teaching of the Dhamma (imāya madhurāya ojavantiyā dhammadesanāya), from the time of hearing (sutakālato paṭṭhāya), he was able to sleep (niddaṃ labhi).

He showed great honor (mahāsakkāraṃ akāsi) to the Triple Gem (tiṇṇaṃ ratanānaṃ).

There was no one equal to this king (iminā raññā sadiso nāhosi) in possessing the faith of a worldling (pothujjanikāya saddhāya samannāgato nāma).

In the future (anāgate pana), he will become a paccekabuddha named Vijitāvī (vijitāvī nāma paccekabuddho hutvā) and attain final Nirvāṇa (parinibbāyissatīti).

This is what the Blessed One said (idamavoca bhagavā).

The monks, delighted (attamanā te bhikkhū), rejoiced at the Blessed One's statement (bhagavato bhāsitaṃ abhinandunti).
